CBAP-Roadmap.title: CBAP Roadmap (13 weeks)
CBAP-Roadmap.content:
CBAP 3-Month Learning Roadmap (13 weeks × 10 h ≈ 130 h)
Context
A high-level CBAP study roadmap based on current (2026) exam facts: 3 months at 10 hours a week. Industry guidance is 120–160 study hours over 3–4 months, so 130 hours is on target, with little slack. It is the backbone of the 75-lesson course.
Exam facts (from the IIBA CBAP Handbook, May 2026)

120 questions, 210 minutes. Multiple choice, scenario-based and case-study questions. You take it online with a remote proctor or at a PSI test center.
Based on BABOK® Guide v3. IIBA also lists the Business Analysis Standard as a study resource. There is no v4 exam yet.
Blueprint weighting:
















































#Knowledge Area%≈ Qs1BA Planning & Monitoring (BAPM)14%172Elicitation & Collaboration (E&C)12%143Requirements Life Cycle Mgmt (RLCM)15%184Strategy Analysis (SA)15%185Requirements Analysis & Design Definition (RADD)30%366Solution Evaluation (SE)14%17

Eligibility: 7,500 BA work hours in the last 10 years, with at least 900 hours in 4 of the 6 KAs; 35 professional development (PD) hours in the last 4 years; 2 references.
Application and exam timing: the application is valid for 1 year, and you get up to 3 exam attempts in that year. Each exam purchase gives you 6 months to sit the exam.

Roadmap
Phase 0: Admin (week 1, runs alongside study)

Join IIBA. Membership gives you free access to BABOK v3 and the Standard on KnowledgeHub, and lowers the fees.
If you don’t have 35 PD hours yet, enroll in an IIBA-endorsed CBAP prep course. It covers the PD hours and fits into weeks 2–8.
Start the application and the BA Development Log now, because an audit can take time. Book the exam for about week 13 or 14 to lock in the deadline.

Phase 1: Foundation (weeks 1–2, 20 h)

BABOK Ch 1–2: the BA Core Concept Model (BACCM: Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context), key terms, requirements classification and stakeholder roles.
Skim Ch 9 (Underlying Competencies) and the Ch 3–8 structure. Every task follows the same pattern: purpose → inputs → elements → guidelines/tools → techniques → stakeholders → outputs.
Take a diagnostic test (about 50 questions) to find your baseline and weak KAs.
Build an input/output flow map across all KAs. It’s the backbone of the “what comes next” questions.

Phase 2: Knowledge Area deep dive (weeks 3–9, 70 h)
Follow the BABOK lifecycle order. Study each KA’s related Ch 10 techniques in the same week.








































WeekFocusKey outputs / techniques to master3BAPM (14%)BA approach, stakeholder engagement, governance, information management, performance improvement. Techniques: stakeholder list/map/personas, RACI, estimation, lessons learned4E&C (12%)Prepare, conduct and confirm elicitation; communicate BA information; stakeholder collaboration. Techniques: interviews, workshops, focus groups, observation, surveys, document analysis, prototyping5RLCM (15%)Trace, maintain, prioritize and assess changes; approve requirements. Techniques: MoSCoW and other prioritization, traceability, backlog management, reviews, decision analysis6SA (15%)Current state, future state, risks and change strategy. Techniques: SWOT, business model canvas, root cause/fishbone, benchmarking, gap analysis, business case7–8RADD (30%, two weeks)Specify and model requirements, verify and validate, requirements architecture, design options, potential value and recommended solution. Techniques: data/process/use case/state/sequence modelling, user stories, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements, glossary, data dictionary9SE (14%)Measure performance, analyze measures, assess solution and enterprise limitations, recommend actions to increase value. Techniques: metrics/KPIs, balanced scorecard, vendor assessment
Every week in this phase ends with a 40-question KA quiz. Target ≥ 75% before moving on, and log every miss.
Phase 3: Techniques and perspectives consolidation (week 10, 10 h)

Build a 50-technique matrix: purpose, usage context and which KAs use each technique. Ch 10 accounts for about a third of question content.
BABOK Ch 11 perspectives: Agile, BI, IT, Business Architecture, BPM. They often appear in case-study context.
Re-read the Ch 9 Underlying Competencies.

Phase 4: Exam simulation and gap closing (weeks 11–13, 30 h)

Weeks 11–12: 2–3 full 120-question, 3.5-hour timed mocks under exam conditions. After each mock, spend about 3 h reviewing every wrong and every guessed answer against the BABOK text.
Focus on case studies: long scenarios where several answers look right and you pick the best one, the most “BABOK-correct” answer.
Week 13: one final mock of at least 80% as your go/no-go signal. Do light review only (input/output map, technique matrix, glossary) and rest before exam day.

Weekly rhythm (10 h)

Weekdays, 5 × 1 h: about 40 minutes of BABOK reading and notes, then about 20 minutes of flashcards or 10 practice questions.
Weekend, 2 × 2.5 h: techniques deep dive, the weekly quiz and error-log review.
Time split across the whole plan: about 55% reading and notes, 30% practice questions, 15% review and spaced repetition.

Recommended resources

Core: the BABOK® Guide v3 (read it at least once, fully) and the IIBA Business Analysis Standard.
Study guides (pick these two):

CBAP Certification Study Guide v3.0 by Richard & Elizabeth Larson (Watermark Learning). The most-reviewed CBAP guide, with plain-English explanations for each KA and task. Use it alongside BABOK in weeks 1–10.
CCBA® and CBAP® Certifications Study Guide by Esta Lessing (Packt, 2020), if you own it. Aligned to BABOK v3, with exam tips, scenarios and practice questions. Use it for KA-end review and weeks 11–13.


Question banks: use one quality simulator with case studies and at least 1,000 questions, such as Adaptive US or Watermark Learning/IIL, plus Udemy CBAP mock exams.
Community: your local IIBA chapter study group, which you can find through IIBA Chapter Events.

Milestones / checkpoints

End of week 2: diagnostic done, flow map drafted, application started.
End of week 9: every KA quiz at 75% or higher.
End of week 12: two full mocks at 75% or higher.
End of week 13: final mock at 80% or higher, then sit the exam.

Verification

Check progress with the weekly quiz scores and mock results. If a KA stays under 70%, move 2–3 hours from the next week to it.
If you’re below 70% on the full mocks by week 12, reschedule the exam. There is flexibility within the 6-month exam window.

Sources

IIBA CBAP Handbook (May 2026)
Adaptive US – How to prepare for CBAP 2026
Adaptive US – CBAP study duration
OpenExamPrep – CBAP exam guide 2026
KnowledgeHut – CBAP exam pattern 2026

about.title: About & Disclaimer
about.content:
What this is
A free, open study companion for the IIBA® CBAP® exam: a 13-week plan, 75 interactive lessons built around a fictional case, and a linked knowledge graph of the BABOK® Guide v3 structure.
Not affiliated with IIBA
IIBA®, BABOK®, CBAP® and CCBA® are registered trademarks of the International Institute of Business Analysis. This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by IIBA. It does not reproduce the BABOK® Guide. It references its structure and page numbers and summarizes ideas in original wording. Get the Guide from iiba.org (free for IIBA members).
Study guides referenced
Page references point to: BABOK® Guide v3 (IIBA, 2015); Esta Lessing, CCBA® and CBAP® Certifications Study Guide (Packt, 2020); Hans Jonasson, CBAP Certification and BABOK Study Guide (CRC Press, 2017). No text from these books is reproduced.
Practice questions
All quiz and mock-exam questions are generated as original practice items. They are not real IIBA exam questions. Use a reputable commercial simulator as well to calibrate.
Credits & license

Course format inspired by Carl Vellotti’s interactive courses (free-ai-courses). No content is copied from them.
Built with Quartz.
Content: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Scripts: MIT. See the repository.

course/module-1/1.1-welcome.title: Lesson 1.1: Welcome to GreenBasket & your CBAP game plan
course/module-1/1.1-welcome.content:
Learn this lesson interactively 
                  
                

This page is the readable version. To be taught it by Claude (Socratic questions, GreenBasket exercises, stakeholder reviews, graded exam drills), clone the repository, open course/ in a terminal, run claude, and type /start 1.1.


Course plan · 1.2 The BACCM: six lenses on every change →
Module 1 · Week 1 · ~60 min in session + ~30 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

SCENARIO
COMPANY
Exam Blueprint
CBAP-Roadmap


Welcome to GreenBasket Markets. It’s your first day as Senior Business Analyst, and your inbox already has a problem in it.
Over the next 13 weeks you’ll do two things at once: pass the CBAP exam, and take GreenBasket’s “Click & Collect” initiative from messy idea to evaluated pilot, using every BABOK knowledge area along the way. The exam tests whether you can apply BABOK in scenarios, and that’s exactly what you’ll practise here.
How this works: I teach a concept, you apply it to GreenBasket, and then I test you with exam-style questions. Your work goes in workspace/, your scores go in progress/, and the whole BABOK lives as a linked knowledge graph in CBAP Knowledge Graph/.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain the CBAP exam format and blueprint weights
Know how the course, commands and files work
Set your exam date and weekly study rhythm
Meet the GreenBasket scenario



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we start: what should I call you, and have you booked (or planned) your exam date yet?



Part 1: The exam you are training for


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Exam Blueprint so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

120 multiple-choice questions in 210 minutes (about 1:45 per question). Questions are scenario-based and case-study based and test application, not recall. Based on BABOK v3.
Blueprint: RADD 30%, RLCM 15%, SA 15%, BAPM 14%, SE 14%, E&C 12%. Techniques (Ch 10) are woven through all of them and underpin roughly a third of question content.
Case-study questions give a long scenario followed by several questions. Several answers are “good” and one is most BABOK-correct.
Eligibility reminder: 7,500 BA hours in 10 years, 900 hours in 4 of the 6 KAs, 35 PD hours, 2 references. The application is valid for 1 year, with up to 3 attempts.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Quick gut check: based on those weights, where should most of your study hours go, and which KA is the smallest?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: RADD at 30% (≈36 questions) is more than double any other KA; E&C is 12% but its techniques appear everywhere, so it is not skippable.



Part 2: How this course works
Key points

Commands: /next continues, /start 2.3 jumps to a lesson, /progress shows the dashboard, /drill RADD 10 runs a quick quiz, /grade mock-1 marks a written exam.
Each lesson follows teach → apply at GreenBasket → exam drill → wrap-up, and takes about 60–90 minutes. Reading assignments come from BABOK, Lessing and Jonasson.
Stakeholder reviewers are available as agents: Elena (sponsor), Marcus (store ops, sceptical), Anil (architect), Priyanka (QA), and a strict CBAP examiner.
The error log is your most valuable file. Every miss gets a “rule to remember”.
The 13-week plan: Foundations (1–2), BAPM (3), E&C (4), RLCM (5), SA (6), RADD (7–8), SE (9), Consolidation (10), Mock exams (11–13).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which of those reviewers do you think will give you the hardest time, and why?



Apply it at GreenBasket: Your first read of the situation
Elena’s kickoff email is waiting. Don’t analyze it formally yet (that’s the next lesson). Just take a BA’s first look.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 01-sponsor-kickoff-email, SCENARIO. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Read the email. In 3 bullets: what is the real need behind it, what are solutions being assumed, and what worries you?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach the answer: separate need (losing share and visit frequency, convenience gap) from assumed solutions (ShelfWise, real-time stock, one-lap rule, slick app). Then create the student’s study contract with their name, exam date, weekly rhythm (for example 5×1 h weekdays + 2×2.5 h weekend), the 3 biggest risks to their study plan, and their answers here. Save the result to workspace/00-study-contract.md and link it: workspace/00-study-contract.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Need: GreenBasket is losing share (18.2% → 14.1%) and visit frequency, driven by a convenience gap versus competitors
Assumed solutions: ShelfWise, “real-time stock”, “slick app”, one-lap picking rule
Worries: Harvest history, store resistance, unrealistic timeline, data quality





                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

Elena already has a vendor in mind. Spotting solutions disguised as requirements is one of the most tested BA instincts.



Set up your progress


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: set student to the student’s name, start_date to today, and exam_date to their target (or 13 weeks from today if unknown). Confirm the dates back to them.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Is the weekly rhythm in your study contract realistic for your life right now? If not, let’s adjust it before week 1 gets busy.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

The CBAP tests application of BABOK v3 in scenarios. Aim for the most BABOK-correct answer.
RADD (30%) is the biggest area. Techniques run across all KAs.
Separate the need from the solutions people bring you. You did it on day one.


Exam rule of thumb: When a stakeholder hands you a solution, the BA move is to understand the underlying need first.

Reading before the next session:

Lessing ch.1–4 (planning for success, exam format), pp.6–45: skim
CBAP Handbook section 6 (exam structure): already summarized in CBAP-Roadmap.md
Admin: join IIBA (free BABOK access), start the CBAP application, check your 35 PD hours



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



CBAP exam length? :: 120 questions, 210 minutes
Largest KA by weight? :: RADD, 30%
CBAP eligibility hours? :: 7,500 BA hours in 10 yrs, 900 in 4 of 6 KAs, 35 PD hours, 2 references



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (1.1) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 60, set current to 1.2, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 1.2: The BACCM: six lenses on every change. The six core concepts that every BABOK task is built on.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready for 1.2? Type /next (or /start 1.2) whenever you are. Short break first is a good idea.



Success Criteria

 Student knows the format and blueprint weights
 Student knows the commands and file layout
 progress.json has name, start date and exam date
 workspace/00-study-contract.md exists
 Student separated need from assumed solutions in the kickoff email


Course plan · 1.2 The BACCM: six lenses on every change →

course/module-1/1.2-baccm.title: Lesson 1.2: The BACCM: six lenses on every change
course/module-1/1.2-baccm.content:
Learn this lesson interactively 
                  
                

This page is the readable version. To be taught it by Claude (Socratic questions, GreenBasket exercises, stakeholder reviews, graded exam drills), clone the repository, open course/ in a terminal, run claude, and type /start 1.2.


← 1.1 Welcome to GreenBasket & your CBAP game plan · Course plan · 1.3 Requirements classification & requirements vs designs →
Module 1 · Week 1 · ~75 min in session + ~30 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

BACCM
Change
Need
Solution
Stakeholder
Value
Context
Key Terms


Every BABOK task, technique and exam scenario can be read through six words: Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context. That’s the Business Analysis Core Concept Model (BACCM).
If you can hold those six in your head, you can dissect any case study question in seconds.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Define all six core concepts in BABOK terms
Explain why no concept is more important than another
Apply the BACCM to a real situation
Use the key terms (business analysis, BA information, design, enterprise, organization, plan, requirement, risk)



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The six concepts


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read BACCM so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Change: a transformation made in response to a need. Need: a problem to solve or an opportunity to pursue. Solution: a particular way of meeting one or more needs within a context.
Stakeholder: anyone (individual or group) connected to the change, the need or the solution. Value: how much something is worth, or how important or useful it is, to a stakeholder in a given context. Context: the surrounding circumstances that shape the change, are shaped by it, and help explain it.
All six are equal, and each is defined by the others. If one changes, re-evaluate the rest.
Value can be tangible or intangible, potential or realized, and absolute or relative. Losses, risks and costs are negative value.
Questions to ask: what kinds of changes? what needs? what solutions? who are the stakeholders? what do they value? what contexts?



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Without looking: which core concept means “how much something is worth or matters to a stakeholder in a given context”, and which one means “a problem to solve or an opportunity to pursue”?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: exact matches. Note “within a context”: value is always relative to a stakeholder and a context.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Distractors often claim one concept (usually Value or Need) is “the most important”. The BABOK says they are all equal.



Part 2: Key terms that the exam uses precisely


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Key Terms so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Business analysis: the practice of making change happen in an enterprise by clarifying needs and proposing solutions that create value for stakeholders.
Requirement = a usable representation of a need. Design = a usable representation of a solution.
Business analysis information = any information, at any level of detail, used as input to or output of BA work. That is why the BABOK says “information”, not just “requirements”.
Enterprise ≠ organization. An enterprise is one or more organizations plus the solutions they use, bounded around the change rather than around a legal entity.
Risk = the effect of uncertainty on the value of a change, a solution, or the enterprise.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Is “a screen mock-up of the pickup check-in page” a requirement or a design? And “customers must be able to tell the store they have arrived”?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: the mock-up represents a solution (design); the arrival need is a requirement (it represents a need).



Apply it at GreenBasket: BACCM analysis of the Click & Collect initiative
Elena wants a one-page view of the initiative. Use the BACCM as your structure.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 01-sponsor-kickoff-email, 04-customer-feedback-q2, 05-market-and-sales-data, 02-harvest-postmortem. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Draft a BACCM table for Click & Collect: one or two lines per concept (Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context). Try it yourself first. Rough is fine.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give specific feedback per concept, then write the polished table plus 3 “questions the BACCM raised” (e.g. whose value? which context constraints?). Save the result to workspace/01-baccm-click-and-collect.md and link it: workspace/01-baccm-click-and-collect.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Change: introduce online ordering with in-store pickup; transform store operations to support picking
Need: stop share loss (18.2→14.1%) and visit-frequency decline (−11%) caused by a convenience gap
Solution: Click & Collect capability (app/web ordering, picking, staging, handover), not yet a specific vendor
Stakeholders: customers (personas), store ops, pickers, sponsor, CFO, IT, compliance, union, vendors
Value: tangible (5% online share, basket retention) and intangible (reputation, convenience); negative value = cost, store burden, risk
Context: Harvest failure, 82% inventory accuracy, union rules, alcohol and cold-chain regulation, competitor moves





                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type elena-sponsor, giving it the path workspace/01-baccm-click-and-collect.md and ask for a sponsor reaction to the BACCM one-pager. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]


                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

The BACCM exposed that the “solution” in Elena’s email (ShelfWise) was chosen before the context (inventory accuracy, union) was understood. That is exactly what killed Harvest.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: BACCM definitions and application, key terms (requirement vs design, enterprise vs organization, BA information, risk).
Mix: 5 scenario, 3 definition.
Build distractors from these traps: claiming one core concept is most important; confusing need with solution; confusing enterprise with organization; value only tangible.
Log to scores.csv with ka=FND and topic=baccm.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Six equal core concepts: Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context.
Requirement ↔ need; design ↔ solution.
Value is always to a stakeholder, within a context, and can be negative.


Exam rule of thumb: If an answer option says one core concept matters more than the others, it is wrong.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK ch.1 (pp.1–10) and 2.1–2.2 (pp.12–16)
Lessing ch.5, pp.46–55



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



BACCM six concepts? :: Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context
Requirement vs design? :: Requirement = usable representation of a need; design = usable representation of a solution
Define risk (BABOK) :: The effect of uncertainty on the value of a change, a solution, or the enterprise



                  
                  What the instructor does

                  Your turn

 Student can classify a statement as requirement vs design

Module 1 · Week 1 · ~75 min in session + ~30 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Requirements Classification Schema
Requirements and Designs
Business Requirements
Non-Functional Requirements Analysis


Tom, the PM, has pasted 20 “requirements” into a spreadsheet and asked you to “sort them out”. Half of them aren’t requirements at all.
Today you learn the classification schema that the exam uses constantly: business → stakeholder → solution (functional / non-functional) → transition.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Classify requirements into the four BABOK types plus functional/non-functional
Spot designs disguised as requirements
Explain why transition requirements are special



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The four types


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Requirements Classification Schema so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Business requirements: goals, objectives and outcomes. Why the change was initiated. They can be enterprise-wide, business-area or initiative level.
Stakeholder requirements: needs of stakeholders that must be met to achieve the business requirements. The bridge between business and solution requirements.
Solution requirements: capabilities and qualities of the solution. Functional = behaviour and information managed. Non-functional (quality of service) = conditions under which it must remain effective, or qualities it must have.
Transition requirements: capabilities and conditions needed only to get from the current state to the future state, such as data conversion, training and business continuity. Temporary.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Classify these: (a) “Online sales reach 5% of total within 2 years”, (b) “Store managers need to see today’s pickup orders by slot”, (c) “The pick list is sorted by aisle sequence”, (d) “Pages load within 2 s for 95% of requests”, (e) “Train 200 store staff before go-live”.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: a = business (outcome, why); b = stakeholder (a need of a group); c = solution-functional; d = solution-non-functional; e = transition (temporary).




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Training and data migration are transition requirements, not non-functional. And “temporary” is the tell.



Part 2: Requirements vs designs, and asking “why?”


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Requirements and Designs so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Requirements focus on the need; designs focus on the solution. The same techniques elicit both, and a requirement can lead to a design that uncovers more requirements.
BABOK tasks that say “requirements” (e.g. Trace, Specify and Model) include designs too.
Stakeholders often present a solution to an assumed need. The BA keeps asking why until the need is clear.
Example: “Use a React Native app with ShelfWise APIs” is a design or technology choice, not a requirement.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Elena wants “real-time stock for every product”. Ask “why?” twice. What need might sit underneath?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: the underlying need is order accuracy and customer trust (avoid unavailable items), which could be met by other designs such as a stock-confidence indicator plus substitution preferences.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Sort Tom’s spreadsheet
Tom’s draft list is a mix of goals, needs, features, designs and wishes.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 11-draft-requirements-v0. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Classify R-01 to R-20 by type (business / stakeholder / solution-functional / solution-NFR / transition), and mark any that are really designs or not requirements at all. Do at least 10 yourself, and I’ll check them.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Check each classification and explain disagreements. Produce a table: ID | type | design? | why | note. Save the result to workspace/02-requirements-classification.md and link it: workspace/02-requirements-classification.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


R-20 “Reduce customer churn” = business requirement (too vague to be measurable yet)
R-03 React Native + ShelfWise = design/technology constraint, not a requirement
R-15 staff training and R-16 migrate phone-order customers = transition
R-18 availability and R-01 “fast/user-friendly” = NFR (R-01 not measurable)
R-05, R-09, R-10, R-12, R-14, R-17, R-19 = functional (R-19 is also a constraint from compliance)
R-04 one-lap rule = a design constraint from the sponsor; ask why





                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type anil-architect, giving it the path workspace/02-requirements-classification.md and ask which items are designs rather than requirements, and which are infeasible. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]


                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

Several “High” priorities came from one person, with no link to a business objective. You will fix that properly in RLCM (prioritization) and RADD (verify and validate).



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: classifying requirements (business, stakeholder, solution-functional, solution-non-functional, transition) and requirement vs design.
Mix: mostly “classify this statement” scenarios.
Build distractors from these traps: training/migration labelled non-functional; business requirement vs stakeholder requirement; design presented as requirement; NFR vs functional for security/audit features.
Log to scores.csv with ka=FND and topic=req-classification.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Four types: business (why), stakeholder (needs of groups), solution (functional plus NFR), transition (temporary).
Requirements ↔ need; designs ↔ solution; keep asking why.
Designs and technology choices hide inside requirement lists. Flag them.


Exam rule of thumb: If it disappears once the change is complete (training, conversion, parallel run), it is a transition requirement.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 2.3 and 2.5, pp.16 and 19–20
Lessing ch.5 pp.59–63
Jonasson ch.3 pp.25–26



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



Transition requirements? :: Temporary capabilities/conditions to move from current to future state (data conversion, training, business continuity)
Stakeholder requirements bridge… :: business requirements and solution requirements
NFR also called? :: Quality of service requirements



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (1.3) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 75, set current to 1.4, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 1.4: Stakeholders: the 11 generic roles. Who is who, in BABOK terms, at GreenBasket.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready for 1.4? Type /next (or /start 1.4) whenever you are. Short break first is a good idea.



Success Criteria

 Student classified at least 10 of the 20 requirements correctly
 Student identified designs inside the list
 workspace/02-requirements-classification.md created
 Drill completed and logged

Module 1 · Week 1 · ~60 min in session + ~30 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Stakeholder Roles
Sponsor
Domain Subject Matter Expert
Implementation Subject Matter Expert
Regulator
End User
STAKEHOLDERS


The BABOK lists 11 generic stakeholder roles. The exam loves questions like “who should approve…?” or “which stakeholder is most likely to…?“. Get the roles crisp, and a lot of questions become easy.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Name and define the 11 generic stakeholder roles
Map real people to roles (one person, many roles)
Distinguish domain SME and implementation SME, and sponsor and project manager



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The 11 roles


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Stakeholder Roles so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Business analyst, customer, domain SME, end user, implementation SME, operational support, project manager, regulator, sponsor, supplier, tester.
Sponsor: initiates the effort, authorizes the work, controls budget and scope. Project manager: manages the work, balancing scope, budget, schedule, resources, quality and risk.
Domain SME = in-depth knowledge of the business topic or need. Implementation SME = specialized knowledge of building or implementing solution components (architect, developer, DBA, trainer, change manager…).
Regulator: defines and enforces standards (legislation, governance, audit). This can be internal (e.g. compliance or audit) or external.
Supplier: outside the organization, provides products or services. Operational support: day-to-day running (help desk, release manager). Tester: verifies the solution meets requirements (QA).
One individual can fill several roles, and any stakeholder can be a source of requirements, assumptions or constraints.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

A trainer who will teach pickers the new handheld process: which role? And the internal auditor who checks alcohol-sale logs?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: trainer = implementation SME (BABOK lists trainers and organizational change consultants there); internal auditor = regulator.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

The exam often swaps sponsor and project manager. Budget and scope authority = sponsor.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Map GreenBasket’s people to BABOK roles
Before you can plan stakeholder engagement (week 3), you need to know who plays which role.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim STAKEHOLDERS, COMPANY. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Build a table: person/group → BABOK role(s) → why. Include at least: Elena, David, Marcus, Rosa, Kim, Anil, Helen, Janet, the union, Tom, Priyanka, Dev, Lily, Ben, the customer personas, and the three vendors. Who plays more than one role?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Validate the mapping, challenge any mistakes (e.g. Janet = regulator (internal); Rosa = domain SME and end-user representative; the union = not a generic BABOK role, but a stakeholder with influence, relevant to the regulator/HR context). Save the table. Save the result to workspace/03-stakeholder-roles.md and link it: workspace/03-stakeholder-roles.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Elena = sponsor; David = sponsor-adjacent decision maker (budget approval)
Marcus, Rosa, Ben, Owen, Lily, Nadia = domain SMEs; Rosa and Kim also end users
Anil, Helen = implementation SMEs; vendors = suppliers (and implementation SMEs during build)
Janet + state agencies + PCI = regulators
Tom = project manager; Priyanka = tester; Dev = operational support; personas = customers




Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: the 11 generic stakeholder roles and their responsibilities.
Mix: scenario “which role” questions.
Build distractors from these traps: sponsor vs project manager; domain SME vs implementation SME; supplier vs customer; regulator only external.
Log to scores.csv with ka=FND and topic=stakeholder-roles.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

11 generic roles. One person can hold several.
Sponsor authorizes and funds; PM manages the work.
Domain SME knows the business; implementation SME knows how to build it.


Exam rule of thumb: Budget or scope authority → sponsor. Standards enforcement (even internal) → regulator.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 2.4, pp.16–19
Lessing ch.5 pp.55–58



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



Who authorizes work and controls budget/scope? :: Sponsor
Trainer, solution architect, DBA are… :: Implementation SMEs
Help desk, release manager are… :: Operational support



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (1.4) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 60, set current to 1.5, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 1.5: Anatomy of a BABOK task & how to study the Guide. The 8-part structure behind all 30 tasks, and how to read the BABOK efficiently.


                  
                  Your turn

Module 1 · Week 1 · ~90 min in session + ~60 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Plan Business Analysis Approach
Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring
00 CBAP Knowledge Graph
Technique-Task Matrix


All 30 BABOK tasks share one skeleton: Purpose, Description, Inputs, Elements, Guidelines & Tools, Techniques, Stakeholders, Outputs. Once you see it, the 500-page guide becomes a well-organized database. It’s also how your knowledge graph is built.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Name the 8 parts of every task and what each tells you
Tell inputs apart from guidelines and tools
Navigate the knowledge graph and the BABOK efficiently
Know the 6 KAs, their 30 tasks and the order they are usually studied in



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The task skeleton


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Plan Business Analysis Approach so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose: why the task exists. Memorize one sentence per task; exam options paraphrase it.
Inputs: information consumed and transformed by the task (often with a state, e.g. “Requirements (verified)”). Outputs: what the task produces.
Guidelines and tools: information that shapes how the task is done but isn’t transformed (e.g. the Business Analysis Approach guides many tasks).
Elements: the key concepts or activities of the task. Techniques: how you might do it. Stakeholders: who typically takes part.
The BABOK is not a sequential process. Tasks can be done in any order, iteratively and concurrently.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

In Plan Business Analysis Approach, “Needs” is an input and “Business Analysis Performance Assessment” is a guideline. What is the difference in plain words?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: inputs are transformed into outputs; guidelines and tools inform or constrain the work without being transformed.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Questions ask “which is an INPUT to task X?” and list guidelines as distractors.



Part 2: Map of the territory


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Technique-Task Matrix so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

6 KAs and 30 tasks: BAPM (5), E&C (5), RLCM (5), SA (4), RADD (6), SE (5).
KAs are not phases. For example, Strategy Analysis can happen before, during and after a project.
50 techniques. Some are used everywhere (Interviews, Workshops, Document Analysis, Risk Analysis and Management), others in only one or two tasks.
Perspectives (Agile, BI, IT, Business Architecture, BPM) are lenses. Underlying competencies are the BA’s skills.
Study method: for each task, know the purpose, element names, inputs and outputs (with states), 3–5 signature techniques, and key stakeholders.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which KA has only 4 tasks, and which has 6?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: SA = 4 (Analyze Current State, Define Future State, Assess Risks, Define Change Strategy); RADD = 6.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Build your one-page task card template
You will fill one task card per task over the next weeks. They are your revision sheets for weeks 11–13.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim Plan Business Analysis Approach. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Using the Plan Business Analysis Approach note, fill in a task card: purpose (in your own words), elements, inputs, guidelines, top 5 techniques, stakeholders, outputs, and “who uses my output next”. What surprised you?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Check the card against the note, correct any wrong names, and save it as the first card. Include a blank template at the top of the file for future cards. Save the result to workspace/task-cards.md and link it: workspace/task-cards.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Purpose (in our words): Decide how business analysis will be carried out on this initiative: the overall method, its formality, the activities, their timing, and how the approach gets agreed.
Elements: planning approach, formality and level of detail, BA activities, timing, complexity and risk, acceptance
Input: Needs; output: Business Analysis Approach, used by 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.5, 6.1…




Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: task structure (inputs vs guidelines vs outputs), KA/task counts, BABOK as non-sequential, perspectives and competencies as concepts.
Build distractors from these traps: guideline listed as input; KAs treated as sequential phases; wrong task-to-KA mapping.
Log to scores.csv with ka=FND and topic=babok-structure.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Every task: purpose, description, inputs, elements, guidelines and tools, techniques, stakeholders, outputs.
Inputs are transformed; guidelines shape the work.
KAs are not phases. Tasks are iterative and concurrent.


Exam rule of thumb: Know each output’s state label. It often decides between two otherwise-good options.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 1.4 Structure (pp.3–10)
Lessing ch.3 Study Tools (pp.31–40)
Jonasson ch.2–3 (pp.11–31): skim for context



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



Eight parts of every BABOK task? :: Purpose, Description, Inputs, Elements, Guidelines and Tools, Techniques, Stakeholders, Outputs
Tasks per KA? :: BAPM 5, E&C 5, RLCM 5, SA 4, RADD 6, SE 5
Are KAs sequential phases? :: No, tasks can be performed in any order, iteratively and concurrently



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (1.5) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 90, set current to 1.6, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 1.6: Diagnostic exam (50 questions). Find your baseline. No pressure, no studying for it.


                  
                  Your turn

Module 1 · Week 2 · ~100 min in session + ~0 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Exam Blueprint
Commonly Confused Concepts
BABOK Input-Output Flow


Today is about data, not ego. A 50-question diagnostic across all KAs shows where you start. Most people score 45–60% before studying, and that’s normal.
Treat it like the real thing: timed (75 minutes), no notes, and honest guesses marked with a ”?“.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Establish a baseline score by KA
Practise exam pacing (about 1.5 min per question)
Start the error log with real data



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Do you have 75 uninterrupted minutes now? If not, we can generate the exam and you take it later.



Generate the exam


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Read the knowledge-graph notes you need (KA notes, the Commonly Confused Concepts note, and the I/O Flow note), then write 50 original CBAP-style questions to exams/diagnostic.md:



Distribution by blueprint: RADD 15, RLCM 8, SA 7, BAPM 7, SE 7, E&C 6.
Mix: about 60% scenario-based (including one mini case study with 4 linked questions), 20% “which input/output/technique”, 20% definitions and concepts.
Each question: number, KA tag hidden (don’t show the KA to the student), 4 options A–D, exactly one best answer.
Write the key to exams/.keys/diagnostic-key.md: number | answer | KA | task/technique | type | 2-line rationale | knowledge-graph note path.
Create exams/diagnostic-answers.md with lines 1:  … 50:  for the student to fill in (letter, plus ? if guessing).

Tell the student the exam is ready and link exams/diagnostic.md and exams/diagnostic-answers.md. Don’t open the key file or reveal answers.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Start your 75-minute timer. Answer in diagnostic-answers.md, add ? to guesses, and tell me when you’re done.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Run the same procedure as the /grade diagnostic command: score it, write exams/diagnostic-report.md, and append misses to the error log and per-KA rows to scores.csv.



Debrief
Share the headline: total %, by-KA table, and time used. Normalize the result: a baseline is a starting point, not a verdict.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Looking at your by-KA scores, which result surprised you most?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Point out the two weakest KAs and the most common confusion pattern. Note them in progress.json weak_topics. Tell them lesson 1.7 will turn this into a personal focus plan.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

You now have a baseline by KA.
Guesses count as misses in the error log. That’s where learning happens.
Pacing target: about 1:45 per question on the real exam.


Exam rule of thumb: On test day, flag and move on after 2 minutes. Never burn 5 minutes on one question.



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (1.6) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 100, set current to 1.7, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 1.7: Diagnostic review & your personal focus plan. Turn your diagnostic into a personal plan.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready for 1.7? Type /next (or /start 1.7) whenever you are. Short break first is a good idea.



Success Criteria

 exams/diagnostic.md and answers exist
 Diagnostic graded; report written
 Error log and scores.csv populated
 Weak KAs recorded in progress.json

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

progress/error-log.md
progress/scores.csv
Commonly Confused Concepts
Also read exams/diagnostic-report.md if it exists.


Your diagnostic misses are the most valuable data you have. Today we sort them into knowledge gaps, confusions and misreads, because each needs a different fix.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Classify errors by root cause
Learn the 14 most commonly confused BABOK pairs
Adjust the study plan to your weak spots



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Three kinds of wrong
Key points

Knowledge gap: you didn’t know the fact (e.g. which task outputs Solution Scope). Fix: study plus flashcards.
Confusion: you mixed up two similar concepts (verify/validate, solution/enterprise limitation). Fix: contrast tables.
Misread or over-thinking: you knew it but answered from “real life” or missed a word like FIRST, BEST, NOT. Fix: exam technique.
BABOK answers beat real-life answers. The exam asks what the BABOK says a BA should do.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Look at your error log: which of the three types dominates for you?



Part 2: The confusion hit-list


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Commonly Confused Concepts so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Walk through the pairs most relevant to the student’s misses (verify vs validate, confirm vs verify, solution vs enterprise limitation, change strategy vs solution scope, business requirements vs business objectives, focus groups vs workshops…).
For each pair: a one-line distinction and a GreenBasket example.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Quick-fire: I describe a situation and you name which side of the pair it is. Ready?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: run 5 rapid quick-fire items drawn from the student’s confused pairs, answered in chat.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Your personal focus plan
Combine the diagnostic data with the 13-week plan.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim progress/error-log.md, CBAP-Roadmap. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Tell me: your 2 weakest KAs, your top 3 confusions, and how many extra minutes per week you could give those areas.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Write a focus plan: baseline table, target by week 9 (≥75% per KA) and week 12 (≥80% on a mock), the extra drills to add (e.g. /drill RADD 10 every Sunday), and which lessons deserve extra time. Update weak_topics in progress.json. Save the result to workspace/04-personal-focus-plan.md and link it: workspace/04-personal-focus-plan.md.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: re-test of the student’s diagnostic misses with fresh questions on the same concepts.
Log to scores.csv with ka=ALL and topic=diagnostic-retest.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Diagnose why you missed, not just what.
Contrast pairs kill confusion errors.
BABOK logic beats real-life habit in exam answers.


Exam rule of thumb: Underline FIRST / BEST / MOST / NOT / EXCEPT in every question stem.

Lessing ch.4 What to Expect From the Exam (pp.41–45)
Review the Commonly Confused Concepts note once more

Module 1 · Week 2 · ~90 min in session + ~30 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

BABOK Input-Output Flow
Requirements
Elicitation Results
Business Analysis Approach
Change Strategy
Solution Scope


Many exam questions are secretly asking: “Which task produced this, and which task uses it next?” Today you learn the backbone: the 38 formal handoffs between tasks and the “state” labels that travel with requirements.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Trace the main input/output chains across KAs
Know the requirement and elicitation-result states
Recognize the “hub” outputs that guide many tasks



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The hub outputs


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Business Analysis Approach, Change Strategy, Solution Scope so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

BAPM outputs (Business Analysis Approach, Stakeholder Engagement Approach, Governance Approach, Information Management Approach, BA Performance Assessment) guide almost everything else.
Strategy Analysis outputs (Current State Description, Future State Description, Business Objectives, Potential Value, Risk Analysis Results, Change Strategy, Solution Scope) guide RADD and SE.
Needs enter from outside (3.1, 3.2, 4.1, 6.1). “(external)” inputs: Performance Objectives (3.5) and Implemented Solution (8.1, 8.3, 8.4).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which task produces Solution Scope, and name two tasks that use it?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: produced by 6.4 Define Change Strategy (together with Change Strategy); used as input by 7.4 and as a guideline by many tasks (5.3, 5.4, 5.5, 7.1, 7.3, 7.5, 7.6, 8.x).



Part 2: The state chains


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Requirements, Elicitation Results so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Elicitation Results: 4.2 → unconfirmed, 4.3 → confirmed, 7.1 accepts any state.
Requirements: 7.1 → specified and modelled → 7.2 verified → 5.5 approves verified requirements. 7.3 → validated. 7.5 uses validated, prioritized requirements. 5.1 → traced, 5.2 → maintained, 5.3 → prioritized, 5.5 → approved.
Designs follow the same RLCM states (traced, maintained, prioritized, approved).
Solution Evaluation chain: 8.1 Solution Performance Measures → 8.2 Solution Performance Analysis → 8.3 Solution Limitation and 8.4 Enterprise Limitation → 8.5 Recommended Actions.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Approve Requirements needs requirements in which state: validated or verified?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: verified: approval follows quality checking. Validated requirements feed design options.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Swapping “verified” and “validated” in the input of Approve Requirements is a classic distractor.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Draw the backbone from memory
Recall beats re-reading. Build the map without looking, then compare it with the graph note.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim BABOK Input-Output Flow. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Without opening the note: list as many “task → output → next task” handoffs as you can in 10 minutes. Aim for 15 or more.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Compare with the I/O Flow note: count correct ones, list the missing and wrong ones, and save a personal “handoff map” with a Mermaid diagram of the main chain (BAPM approaches → E&C results → SA outputs → RADD states → RLCM states → SE chain). Mark the ones they missed with ⚠️. Save the result to workspace/05-my-io-backbone.md and link it: workspace/05-my-io-backbone.md.




                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

Most people forget that Business Requirements come out of Analyze Current State, not Define Future State. Did you?



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: input/output handoffs, state labels, which task produces or consumes a given output.
Build distractors from these traps: verified vs validated as input to Approve; Business Requirements produced by Define Future State; Solution Scope produced by RADD; Elicitation Results (confirmed) produced by Conduct Elicitation.
Log to scores.csv with ka=FND and topic=io-flow.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

BAPM approaches and SA outputs are hub guidelines.
Know the states: unconfirmed → confirmed; specified and modelled → verified / validated → prioritized → approved.
The SE chain: measures → analysis → limitations → recommended actions.


Exam rule of thumb: “What should the BA do next?” means: find which task consumes the output you currently have.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK input/output diagrams at the start of each KA chapter (3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0): study the figures only
Appendix B Techniques to Task Mapping (p.457): skim



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



Business Requirements are output by… :: 6.1 Analyze Current State
Approve Requirements input state? :: Requirements (verified)
Define Change Strategy outputs? :: Change Strategy and Solution Scope
Define Design Options input requirements state? :: Requirements (validated, prioritized)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (1.8) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 90, set current to 1.9, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 1.9: Underlying competencies & perspectives: a primer. The skills and lenses that frame every scenario.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready for 1.9? Type /next (or /start 1.9) whenever you are. Short break first is a good idea.

Module 1 · Week 2 · ~60 min in session + ~45 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Underlying Competencies
Analytical Thinking and Problem Solving
Interaction Skills
Perspectives
The Agile Perspective


Case studies often hide a competency question (“the BA is demonstrating…”) or a perspective (“in an agile context, the BA should…”). Today is a primer. We go deep in week 10.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Name the 6 competency groups and a few competencies in each
Explain what a perspective is and name the 5
Recognize competency and perspective cues in scenarios



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Underlying competencies


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Underlying Competencies so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Six groups: Analytical Thinking and Problem Solving (creative, decision making, learning, problem solving, systems, conceptual, visual thinking), Behavioural Characteristics (ethics, personal accountability, trustworthiness, organization and time management, adaptability), Business Knowledge (business acumen, industry, organization, solution, methodology), Communication Skills (verbal, non-verbal, written, listening), Interaction Skills (facilitation, leadership and influencing, teamwork, negotiation and conflict resolution, teaching), Tools and Technology (office productivity, BA tools, communication tools).
Each competency has a purpose, a definition and effectiveness measures.
Systems thinking = the whole and how the parts interact. Conceptual thinking = fitting details into the bigger picture and connecting seemingly unrelated information.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Rosa tells you about a workaround in her store, and you immediately see how it will affect pick accuracy, customer trust and store labour budgets. Which competency is that?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: systems thinking: understanding how changing one component affects the whole system.



Part 2: Perspectives


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Perspectives so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

A perspective is a lens for BA work in a specific context: Agile, Business Intelligence, Information Technology, Business Architecture, Business Process Management.
Each describes change scope, BA scope, methodologies, underlying competencies, and impact on KAs.
Agile: continuous, just-in-time elaboration, backlog, short iterations. BI: data to insight. IT: impact on systems. BA (business architecture): enterprise models. BPM: process improvement.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

GreenBasket’s pilot team works in 2-week sprints from a backlog. Which perspective frames that, and how does it change when requirements are elaborated?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: Agile perspective: requirements elaborated just in time, prioritized backlog, continuous planning.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: identifying competencies from behaviours and matching perspectives to contexts.
Build distractors from these traps: systems vs conceptual thinking; facilitation vs leadership; business acumen vs industry knowledge; BPM vs business architecture perspective.
Log to scores.csv with ka=COMP and topic=competency-perspective-primer.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

6 competency groups. Know the names and one example behaviour each.
5 perspectives are lenses, not methods.
Scenario verbs (“facilitated”, “negotiated”, “visualized”) hint at the competency.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK ch.9 intro plus 9.1 (pp.185–193)
BABOK ch.11 intro (p.367): skim each perspective’s first page
Jonasson 3.4–3.5 (pp.26–31)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



6 underlying competency groups? :: Analytical Thinking & Problem Solving; Behavioural Characteristics; Business Knowledge; Communication Skills; Interaction Skills; Tools & Technology
5 perspectives? :: Agile, Business Intelligence, Information Technology, Business Architecture, Business Process Management



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (1.9) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 60, set current to 1.10, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 1.10: Foundation checkpoint. Lock in the foundations before Knowledge Area deep dives.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready for 1.10? Type /next (or /start 1.10) whenever you are. Short break first is a good idea.



Success Criteria

 Student can name the 6 competency groups
 Student can name the 5 perspectives
 Drill logged

Module 2 · Week 3 · ~80 min in session + ~30 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring
Plan Business Analysis Approach
Business Analysis Approach
Needs


Elena asked for “how you’re going to approach this, and no 80-page documents”. That’s literally 3.1 Plan Business Analysis Approach. This week is BA Planning & Monitoring (BAPM): 14% of the exam, and the KA whose outputs guide almost every other task.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain the purpose and five tasks of BAPM
Explain the 6 elements of Plan Business Analysis Approach
Choose between predictive and adaptive approaches with reasons
Know the input (Needs) and output (Business Analysis Approach)



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: BAPM at a glance


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Five tasks: 3.1 Plan BA Approach, 3.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement, 3.3 Plan BA Governance, 3.4 Plan BA Information Management, 3.5 Identify BA Performance Improvements.
Outputs are approaches: BA Approach, Stakeholder Engagement Approach, Governance Approach, Information Management Approach, plus the BA Performance Assessment. These act as guidelines for most other tasks.
Only two inputs come from outside: Needs, and Performance Objectives (external).
BACCM in BAPM: e.g. Change = how changes to BA results are requested and authorized; Value = performance analysis to keep BA activities producing value.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Name the five BAPM outputs.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: all five with exact names.



Part 2: Plan Business Analysis Approach


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Plan Business Analysis Approach so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Decide how business analysis will be carried out on this initiative: the overall method, its formality, the activities, their timing, and how the approach gets agreed.
Elements: Planning Approach (predictive ↔ adaptive continuum), Formality and Level of Detail of BA deliverables, BA Activities, Timing of BA Work, Complexity and Risk, Acceptance.
Predictive: minimize upfront uncertainty, define before build; suits high risk, regulated contexts, formal sign-off, distributed or outsourced teams. Adaptive: rapid value in short iterations, accepts more uncertainty, lighter documentation, prioritized requirements list.
Formality rises with complexity and risk, regulation, contracts, geographic distribution, outsourcing, staff turnover, formal sign-off, and long-term maintenance needs.
Acceptance: the approach is reviewed and agreed with key stakeholders, such as the sponsor.
Input: Needs. Guidelines include the BA Performance Assessment, business policies, expert judgment, methodologies and frameworks, and the Stakeholder Engagement Approach. Output: Business Analysis Approach.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

GreenBasket has regulated areas (alcohol, cold chain, PCI) but also a tight timeline and a need for store feedback. Predictive, adaptive or a mix? Justify it using two elements.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: a hybrid is defensible. Predictive formality for compliance areas and vendor contracts (formality element, complexity and risk); adaptive iterations with pilot stores for the customer and picker experience (timing element). BABOK explicitly allows different approaches within one initiative.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

“Adaptive means no documentation” is false. It means documentation at the team’s discretion, often produced after implementation for knowledge transfer.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Draft GreenBasket’s Business Analysis Approach (one page)
Elena wants a short, decision-ready approach. Harvest’s failures are your best input.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 01-sponsor-kickoff-email, 02-harvest-postmortem, 08-compliance-memo. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Draft a one-page BA approach covering each of the 6 elements: planning approach, formality and level of detail, BA activities (list them), timing, complexity and risk, and how you’ll get acceptance. Tie at least 3 decisions to lessons from Harvest.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach element by element, then save a polished one-page approach using the element names as headings, plus a “Harvest lessons applied” box. Save the result to workspace/10-ba-approach.md and link it: workspace/10-ba-approach.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Hybrid: predictive for compliance, vendor selection and integration; adaptive sprints for customer and picker experience
Formality: formal sign-off only for compliance-related requirements and the vendor contract; lightweight backlog and models elsewhere
Activities: discovery (store observation, picker interviews), strategy and business case, requirements, vendor evaluation, pilot evaluation
Timing: BA leads the project by 1–2 sprints; strategy work before vendor selection
Complexity and risk: data quality, union, 42 stores, regulation → more store involvement and early risk work
Acceptance: walkthrough with Elena, Marcus and Tom; approval by Elena





                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type elena-sponsor, giving it the path workspace/10-ba-approach.md and ask for a sponsor reaction and whether they would accept it. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]


                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

Harvest had a 212-page specification written in 6 weeks with no store input. Formality without the right stakeholders is not quality.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: BAPM overview and 3.1 Plan Business Analysis Approach (elements, predictive vs adaptive, formality drivers, inputs, guidelines, outputs).
Build distractors from these traps: adaptive = no documentation; approach selected without stakeholder acceptance; Business Analysis Performance Assessment as an input (it is a guideline); confusing BA approach with project management plan.
Log to scores.csv with ka=BAPM and topic=3.1.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

BAPM outputs are guidelines for nearly every other task.
3.1 has 6 elements; the approach can mix predictive and adaptive.
Formality follows risk, regulation, distribution and sign-off needs.


Exam rule of thumb: The BA plans BA work (the approach). The project manager plans the project. Don’t pick answers where the BA writes the project plan.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 3.0–3.1 (pp.21–31)
Lessing ch.6 pp.73–84
Jonasson 4.3.1 (pp.34–48): waterfall, iterative, agile



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



3.1 elements? :: Planning Approach; Formality & Level of Detail; BA Activities; Timing of BA Work; Complexity & Risk; Acceptance
3.1 input? :: Needs
Predictive approaches are preferred when… :: requirements can be defined upfront, implementation risk is high, or stakeholder engagement is difficult



                  
                  What the instructor does

Next up: Lesson 2.2: 3.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement. Stakeholder analysis, collaboration and communication needs, with Marcus.

 Student explained predictive vs adaptive trade-offs
