Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Plan Stakeholder Engagement
Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas
Stakeholder Engagement Approach
STAKEHOLDERS


Harvest “informed” store managers by email a week before trial. Marcus hasn’t forgotten. Today you plan stakeholder engagement properly: 3.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Perform stakeholder analysis (roles, attitudes, decision authority, power and interest)
Define collaboration and communication needs
Use stakeholder lists, maps (onion, power/interest), RACI and personas



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The task


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Plan Stakeholder Engagement so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Work out who the stakeholders are, what they are like, and how the BA will work and communicate with each of them.
Elements: Perform Stakeholder Analysis (identify, roles, attitudes, decision-making authority, level of power or influence), Define Stakeholder Collaboration, Stakeholder Communication Needs (what, format, frequency, level of detail, cultural and geographic considerations).
Inputs: Needs, Business Analysis Approach. Output: Stakeholder Engagement Approach.
Attitudes to analyze: towards the business goals, the solution approach, business analysis itself, collaboration, and the sponsor.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which element would you use to capture “Marcus prefers face-to-face meetings and distrusts slide decks”?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: mostly Stakeholder Communication Needs (format, delivery), with his attitude captured in Perform Stakeholder Analysis.



Part 2: Signature technique: Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Stakeholder List, Map, or Personas so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Stakeholder matrix (influence/power × impact/interest): high/high = work closely, high power/low interest = keep satisfied (ensure needs met), low power/high interest = keep informed, low/low = monitor.
Onion diagram: solution delivery team → affected organizational units → organization/enterprise → external stakeholders (customers, suppliers, regulators).
RACI: Responsible, Accountable (only one), Consulted, Informed.
Personas: fictional characters representing a user type, e.g. “Busy Parent Sam”.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Janet (compliance) has high power but low interest until something touches her domains. Which quadrant, and what engagement strategy?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: keep satisfied: targeted involvement on the six compliance areas, early sight of related requirements, no need for every meeting.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

RACI allows only one Accountable per activity.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Stakeholder Engagement Approach for Click & Collect
Build the approach that would have saved Harvest.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim STAKEHOLDERS, 02-harvest-postmortem, 10-workshop-notes-raw. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Produce: (1) a power/interest map of at least 12 stakeholders, (2) attitude notes for Marcus, Lily, Janet and Kim, (3) a RACI for “approve store-process requirements”, and (4) communication needs for 4 key groups (format, frequency, detail).




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and correct (e.g. one Accountable only; union via HR; pickers must be consulted). Save the full Stakeholder Engagement Approach including a Mermaid quadrant chart or a table. Save the result to workspace/11-stakeholder-engagement-approach.md and link it: workspace/11-stakeholder-engagement-approach.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Manage closely: Elena, Marcus, Rosa (as store voice), Anil
Keep satisfied: David (CFO), Janet, Helen, Nadia/union
Keep informed: Kim and pickers (high interest; empower with a voice), Lily, Ben, Dev, customers (via panels)
Marcus: resistant; engage face-to-face, co-design pilot selection, address funding of pickers
RACI: Accountable = Marcus (store process owner); Responsible = BA; Consulted = Rosa, Kim, Nadia, Janet; Informed = Tom, Priyanka





                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type marcus-store-ops, giving it the path workspace/11-stakeholder-engagement-approach.md and ask for his honest reaction to how stores are engaged. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]


                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

Marcus’s resistance is about funding and respect, not the idea itself. Stakeholder analysis finds the reason behind an attitude.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: 3.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement: elements, attitudes, power/interest, onion diagram, RACI, personas, communication needs.
Build distractors from these traps: more than one Accountable; keep satisfied vs keep informed; Stakeholder Engagement Approach vs Stakeholder Engagement (4.5 output); confusing stakeholder analysis with requirements elicitation.
Log to scores.csv with ka=BAPM and topic=3.2.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Analyze roles, attitudes, decision authority and power/influence.
Plan collaboration and communication needs, tailored per group.
Output: Stakeholder Engagement Approach (the plan). 4.5 later produces Stakeholder Engagement (the result).


Exam rule of thumb: A resistant, high-power stakeholder calls for early, direct engagement and understanding their concerns. Never go around them.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 3.2 (pp.31–36) and 10.43 (pp.344–347)
Lessing pp.84–88 and 427
Jonasson 4.3.2 (pp.49–56): user profiling

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



3.2 elements? :: Perform Stakeholder Analysis; Define Stakeholder Collaboration; Stakeholder Communication Needs
RACI? :: Responsible, Accountable (one only), Consulted, Informed

Governance Approach
02-harvest-postmortem


Harvest had 63 change requests “agreed in corridors” and no owner for approvals. Today you design the rules of the game: 3.3 Plan Business Analysis Governance.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain the 4 elements of governance planning
Design a change control process for BA information
Define decision rights, the prioritization approach and approvals

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The task


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Plan Business Analysis Governance so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Set the rules for decisions about requirements and designs: who decides, how changes are controlled, how priorities are set, and how approvals happen.
Elements: Decision Making (who decides, escalation path), Change Control Process (how changes are requested, what a change request contains, how changes are prioritized, documented and communicated, who does impact analysis, who authorizes), Plan Prioritization Approach (formality, basis and who participates), Plan for Approvals (what is approved, when, by whom, format).
Change request contents: cost and time estimates, benefits, risks, priority, course(s) of action.
Inputs: BA Approach, Stakeholder Engagement Approach. Output: Governance Approach, a guideline for 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which later tasks use the Governance Approach as a guideline?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: 5.3 Prioritize Requirements, 5.4 Assess Requirements Changes, 5.5 Approve Requirements.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

BA governance covers decisions about BA information (requirements and designs), not the whole project governance.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Governance Approach for Click & Collect

Decision rights by requirement domain; escalation to Elena as sponsor
CR fields: description, requester, benefit, cost/time estimate, risk of doing and not doing, priority, affected requirements, recommendation
Change control board weekly: Elena (chair), Tom, Marcus, Anil, BA; Janet for compliance CRs
Prioritization: agreed basis (value, cost, risk, regulatory), workshop-based, with the sponsor as tie-breaker
Approvals: formal sign-off for compliance and vendor contract; sprint-review acceptance for backlog items

Plan Business Analysis Information Management
Information Management Approach
02-harvest-postmortem


Harvest’s spec mixed business needs with screen designs, and nobody could tell why a feature existed. That’s an information management failure. Today: 3.4 Plan BA Information Management.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain the 6 elements of 3.4
Choose the level of abstraction per audience
Plan traceability, reuse, storage and requirements attributes



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The task


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Plan Business Analysis Information Management so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Decide how business analysis information will be organized, detailed, traced, reused, stored and described with attributes.
Elements: Organization of BA Information, Level of Abstraction (by audience and complexity), Plan Traceability Approach, Plan for Requirements Reuse, Storage and Access, Requirements Attributes.
Attributes: absolute reference, author, complexity, ownership, priority, risks, source, stability, status, urgency.
Inputs: BA Approach, Governance Approach, Stakeholder Engagement Approach. Output: Information Management Approach, a guideline for 4.4, 5.1, 5.2 and an input to 7.4.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which attribute would have answered “why does this feature exist?” in Harvest?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: source (and the traceability approach linking requirements to business objectives).




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Information management (3.4, planning storage, traceability and attributes) vs requirements architecture (7.4, how requirements fit together).



Apply it at GreenBasket: Information Management Approach
Decide how Click & Collect’s BA information will be organized so nothing gets lost like in Harvest.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 11-draft-requirements-v0, 02-harvest-postmortem. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.

Decide: how information is organized (by what structure?), levels of abstraction for Elena, stores and vendors, the traceability approach (what traces to what, at what formality), what will be reused (hint: Harvest adapter, the prototype), storage and access (tool, permissions), and the attribute set you will capture for every requirement.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save the approach, including an attribute table with an example requirement (R-17 pick path) fully attributed. Save the result to workspace/13-information-management-approach.md and link it: workspace/13-information-management-approach.md.

Organize by business objective → capability (ordering, picking, staging, handover, loyalty, compliance) → requirements and designs
Abstraction: one-page views for Elena; process models and user stories for stores and vendors
Trace business objectives → stakeholder requirements → solution requirements → test cases; formality higher for compliance
Reuse: Harvest TillMaster adapter requirements, customer prototype insights
Storage: one repository with role-based access; the vendor gets read access to relevant sections





                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

Reuse is an explicit BABOK element: Harvest’s adapter and prototype findings are assets, not waste.

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Identify Business Analysis Performance Improvements
Business Analysis Performance Assessment
Performance Objectives (external)
17-ba-team-retro-notes
Lessons Learned
Metrics and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)


Week 6 of the initiative: your BA team’s retro data is in. 34% of requirements needed rework, approvals take 11 days, and stores rate BA engagement at 3.1/5. Time for 3.5 Identify BA Performance Improvements. Note the target: the BA work, not the solution.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain the 4 elements of 3.5
Define BA performance measures
Recommend preventive, corrective and improvement actions



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The task


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Identify Business Analysis Performance Improvements so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Evaluate how well the business analysis work itself is going, and put improvements in place.
Elements: Performance Analysis, Assessment Measures (accuracy and completeness, knowledge, effectiveness, organizational support, significance, strategic, timeliness), Analyze Results, Recommend Actions for Improvement (preventive, corrective, improvement).
Inputs: BA Approach, Performance Objectives (external). Output: BA Performance Assessment, which feeds back as a guideline into 3.1–3.4 and 4.5.
Techniques: lessons learned (retrospective), metrics and KPIs, root cause analysis, reviews, surveys, interviews.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Is “34% of requirements needed rework” a solution performance measure or a BA performance measure?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: BA performance (accuracy and completeness of BA deliverables). Solution performance measures belong to 8.1.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

BA Performance Assessment (3.5) vs Solution Performance Analysis (8.2).



Apply it at GreenBasket: BA Performance Assessment from the retro
Grace wants an honest assessment and an improvement plan.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 17-ba-team-retro-notes. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Analyze the retro data: which measures are off target, what are the likely root causes, and what actions would you recommend? Label each action as preventive, corrective or improvement.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach it and save a BA Performance Assessment: measures table (plan, actual, variance), root causes (e.g. Friday scheduling, no peer review, unclear approval rights), and actions labelled preventive, corrective or improvement, plus which BAPM output each action updates. Save the result to workspace/14-ba-performance-assessment.md and link it: workspace/14-ba-performance-assessment.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Rework 34% → root cause: compound or vague requirements, no checklist → preventive: peer review with a quality checklist (link to 7.2)
Approval 11 days → unclear decision rights → corrective: update the Governance Approach (3.3)
Store satisfaction 3.1 → sessions on Fridays → corrective: reschedule; update the Stakeholder Engagement Approach (3.2)
Marketing felt shut down → improvement: a structured ideas backlog for Lily





                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

The assessment loops back: it becomes a guideline for 3.1–3.4 and for 4.5. BAPM is a cycle, not a one-off.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: 3.5 elements, BA performance measures vs solution measures, preventive/corrective/improvement actions, the feedback loop.
Build distractors from these traps: BA performance vs solution performance; Performance Objectives (external) produced internally; lessons learned only at project end.
Log to scores.csv with ka=BAPM and topic=3.5.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

3.5 improves BA work itself.
Actions are preventive, corrective or improvement.
Its output feeds back into the other BAPM tasks and into 4.5.


Exam rule of thumb: “How well is the BA work going?” → 3.5. “How well is the solution performing?” → Solution Evaluation.

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Estimation
Item Tracking
Lessons Learned
Reviews
Functional Decomposition
Risk Analysis and Management


Techniques make up about a third of the exam content. Today’s lab covers the ones BAPM leans on. You’ll use them on GreenBasket, not just memorize them.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Apply estimation methods (incl. PERT)
Set up item tracking
Run a lessons-learned review
Know the review types



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Estimation


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Estimation so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Methods: top-down, bottom-up, parametric, rolling wave, Delphi, PERT (three-point: (O + 4M + P) / 6), analogous, historical analysis, expert judgment.
Estimates are ranges with confidence levels and should be revised as information improves (rolling wave).
BA uses: estimating BA effort (3.1), elicitation (4.1), prioritization cost (5.3), change impact (5.4), solution options (6.4, 7.6).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Estimate BA effort for store observation sessions: optimistic 6 days, most likely 9, pessimistic 18. What is the PERT estimate?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: (6 + 36 + 18) / 6 = 10 days.



Part 2: Item tracking, lessons learned, reviews


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Item Tracking, Lessons Learned, Reviews so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Item tracking: capture and assign responsibility for issues, actions, assumptions, constraints, dependencies, defects, enhancements, until resolved. Attributes include ID, description, type, date identified, owner, priority, impact, resolution date, status.
Lessons learned: compile successes, failures and recommendations. Can happen at any point (retrospectives), not only at the end.
Review types: inspection (most formal, checklist), formal walkthrough, single-issue review, informal walkthrough, desk check, pass-around, ad hoc. Roles: author, reviewer, facilitator, scribe.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

The workshop notes had “action items: nobody assigned owners”. Which technique fixes that?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: item tracking: every item gets an owner, status and resolution date.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Issue and action log from the inherited mess
Workshop #1 and the Harvest post-mortem left many open issues with no owners.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 10-workshop-notes-raw, 02-harvest-postmortem. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn

Prepare for Elicitation

Document Analysis
Data Mining


Rosa said it plainly in 2024: “Don’t let head office design this alone again. Talk to Kim.” This week you do elicitation properly. First: 4.1 Prepare for Elicitation.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain E&C’s five tasks and the elicitation-results states
Know the 5 elements of 4.1 and its output
Name the three types of elicitation (collaborative, research, experiments)



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: E&C at a glance


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Elicitation and Collaboration so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Five tasks: 4.1 Prepare for Elicitation, 4.2 Conduct Elicitation, 4.3 Confirm Elicitation Results, 4.4 Communicate BA Information, 4.5 Manage Stakeholder Collaboration.
Elicitation is iterative and ongoing. It isn’t a phase. It draws out, explores and identifies information, which is more than “gathering”.
State flow: Elicitation Activity Plan → Elicitation Results (unconfirmed) → Elicitation Results (confirmed).
Three types of elicitation (4.2): collaborative (direct interaction), research (documents and data), experiments (observation, proofs of concept, prototypes to find unknowns).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Studying the Harvest post-mortem: collaborative, research, or experiment?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: research: systematically discovering and studying information from materials or sources not directly known by stakeholders involved in the change.



Part 2: Prepare for Elicitation


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Prepare for Elicitation so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Get ready for an elicitation activity: its scope, the techniques, the logistics, the materials, and the people taking part.
Elements: Understand the Scope of Elicitation, Select Elicitation Techniques, Set Up Logistics, Secure Supporting Material, Prepare Stakeholders.
Inputs: Needs, Stakeholder Engagement Approach. Guidelines: BA Approach, Business Objectives, Existing BA Information, Potential Value. Output: Elicitation Activity Plan.
Techniques include document analysis, data mining, interviews, brainstorming, estimation, mind mapping, risk analysis, and stakeholder list, map or personas.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Why would you do Document Analysis and Data Mining during preparation, before meeting anyone?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: to build background knowledge, identify gaps and good questions, and respect stakeholder time. Here that means the Harvest post-mortem, SO-12 data and survey stats.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Elicitation Activity Plan: picker and store discovery
Plan elicitation with Riverton Central (Rosa, Kim, pickers) for next Tuesday morning (the retro told you: not Fridays).


                  
                  What the instructor does

                  Your turn 
                  
                

Draft the Elicitation Activity Plan for each of the 5 elements: scope and goals, techniques (and why: interviews, observation, a small workshop?), logistics (time, place, duration), supporting materials, and how you’ll prepare the stakeholders.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save. Emphasize observation for tacit knowledge, interviewing Kim separately so it feels safe to speak (low power), avoiding peak times, bringing the SO-12 form and Kim’s 2024 issue list, and sending an agenda in advance. Save the result to workspace/20-elicitation-activity-plan.md and link it: workspace/20-elicitation-activity-plan.md.

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?

E&C is iterative; results move from unconfirmed to confirmed.
4.1 elements: scope, techniques, logistics, supporting material, prepare stakeholders.

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Conduct Elicitation
Interviews
Observation
Elicitation Results (unconfirmed)
STAKEHOLDERS
02-harvest-postmortem


Today you don’t just read about elicitation. You do it. I’ll play Kim Tran, a picker at Riverton Central. Kim knows exactly why picking failed in Harvest, but only shares it with an interviewer who earns trust and asks good questions.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain the elements of 4.2 (guide the activity, capture outcomes)
Run a structured interview with open and closed questions
Produce Elicitation Results (unconfirmed)



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Conduct Elicitation


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Conduct Elicitation, Interviews so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Run the elicitation activity: draw out and explore information with stakeholders or from sources, and record what comes out of it.
Elements: Guide Elicitation Activity (keep to scope, probe, watch for new information) and Capture Elicitation Outcomes.
Input: Elicitation Activity Plan. Output: Elicitation Results (unconfirmed). 18 techniques are listed, the most of any E&C task.
Interview tips: prepare goals and questions; open questions to explore and closed questions to confirm; build rapport; don’t lead; summarize and confirm at the end.
Observation: active/noticeable (asking questions) vs passive/unnoticeable (just watching). It reveals tacit knowledge and workarounds.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Give me one open question and one closed question you might ask Kim.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: open, e.g. “Walk me through picking a big order on a Saturday”. Closed, e.g. “Did the handhelds last a full shift?“. Avoid leading questions like “The scanners were the main problem, right?“.



Apply it at GreenBasket: The interview (role-play)


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Role-play as Kim Tran (picker, 4 years, low power, high interest, did Harvest trial picks) for the next exchange. Rules for playing Kim:



Start friendly but guarded: “Is this another head-office thing? Last time nobody read my list.”
Share information in proportion to question quality. Open, non-leading questions earn detail; leading or closed-only questions get short answers.
Facts Kim knows (reveal only when asked well): aisle locations wrong after resets; no substitution guidance; handheld battery ~2 h; chilled items warm by the end; Saturday rush; unclear whether picking counts in productivity targets; totes by temperature zone would help; a dedicated early-morning picker schedule works best; 17-year-old evening staff can’t hand over alcohol; a staging cooler is needed; one-lap picking is impossible for orders over 40 items in big stores.
If the student confirms and summarizes at the end, Kim warms up and offers to show them on the shop floor (observation).
Stay in character until the student says “end interview”.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

You’re sitting with Kim in the break room with 30 minutes. Start the interview. Type “end interview” when you’re done.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Step out of character. Debrief: what went well (rapport, open questions, probing, summarizing) and what was missed (list the facts not uncovered). Then write the elicitation results as unconfirmed notes: source, date, technique, verbatim quotes, observations, open questions. Save the result to workspace/21-elicitation-results-kim-unconfirmed.md and link it: workspace/21-elicitation-results-kim-unconfirmed.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Rapport first; acknowledge the ignored 2024 list
Open questions on the end-to-end picking flow; probing on “why” for delays
Captured facts about data, devices, temperature, peaks and incentives
Summarized at the end and asked to observe a pick (experiment/observation)





                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

The unconfirmed results already contradict Rosa’s 2024 interview (“15 minutes”, “stock mostly fine”). Next lesson you confirm which is right.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: 4.2 Conduct Elicitation, interview technique (question types, structured vs unstructured), observation types, capturing outcomes.
Build distractors from these traps: results from 4.2 labelled confirmed; leading questions; passive observation when you need to understand reasons; interviews for large dispersed populations (survey is better).
Log to scores.csv with ka=E&C and topic=4.2.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

4.2 = guide the activity plus capture outcomes; the output is unconfirmed.
Open questions explore; closed questions confirm; never lead.
Observation uncovers tacit knowledge that interviews miss.


Exam rule of thumb: Large, dispersed group → survey. Tacit, hands-on work → observation. Deep individual view → interview. Group consensus → workshop.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 4.2 (pp.61–64), 10.25 Interviews, 10.31 Observation
Jonasson 5.5–5.6 (pp.79–89)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



4.2 output? :: Elicitation Results (unconfirmed)
Active vs passive observation? :: Active/noticeable: observer asks questions during work; passive/unnoticeable: observer watches without interrupting
4.2 elements? :: Guide Elicitation Activity; Capture Elicitation Outcomes



                  
                  What the instructor does

03-store-ops-process-notes


Rosa said picking takes 15 minutes. The store’s own data says 18–41. Kim says it’s worse on Saturdays. The Harvest contractor wrote “confirmed”. Confirming is exactly what they failed to do. Today: 4.3 Confirm Elicitation Results.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain the two elements of 4.3
Distinguish confirm vs verify vs validate
Resolve contradictions between sources



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Confirm Elicitation Results


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Confirm Elicitation Results so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Check that what was elicited is accurate and consistent, by comparing it with sources and with other results.
Elements: Compare Elicitation Results Against Source Information, and Compare Elicitation Results Against Other Elicitation Results.
Input: Elicitation Results (unconfirmed). Guidelines: Elicitation Activity Plan, Existing BA Information. Output: Elicitation Results (confirmed).
Techniques: document analysis, interviews, reviews, workshops.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How is confirming different from verifying requirements (7.2)?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: confirm checks the BA captured information accurately and consistently. Verify checks that specified requirements are well-formed (quality characteristics).




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Answers saying “validate the elicitation results” are usually wrong. Confirm is the BABOK word here.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Reconcile the sources
Three sources disagree about the current process.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 09-interview-transcript-rosa, 03-store-ops-process-notes, workspace/21-elicitation-results-kim-unconfirmed.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Build a comparison: for pick time, stock accuracy, where chilled/frozen go, which till is used, alcohol on phone orders, and who picks and when, note what each source says, the contradiction, and how you would confirm it (which technique, with whom).




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach it and save a confirmation matrix, then a “confirmed results” section for the items that the data or documents settle (e.g. pick times are 18–41 min per the store table; the manual is outdated per Rosa’s own notes). Mark items still needing confirmation with owners. Save the result to workspace/22-elicitation-results-confirmed.md and link it: workspace/22-elicitation-results-confirmed.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Pick time: manual silent, Rosa said 15, the table shows 18–41 → confirmed as 18–41, driven by day of week
Stock accuracy “mostly fine” vs IT 82% (74% fresh) → confirmed not fine for fresh
Frozen goes to the front ice-cream freezer, not the back cooler (margin note) → cold-chain risk to confirm by observation
Alcohol: unwritten head-office rule → confirm with Janet





                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

The Harvest contractor wrote “confirmed” after a single interview. Confirmation means comparing against source information and other results.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: 4.3 Confirm Elicitation Results and the confirm vs verify vs validate distinction.
Build distractors from these traps: confirm = validate; confirmed results produced by 4.2; confirmation requires formal sign-off.
Log to scores.csv with ka=E&C and topic=4.3.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Confirm = accuracy and consistency against sources and other results.
Output: Elicitation Results (confirmed).
Confirm ≠ verify ≠ validate.


Exam rule of thumb: Contradictions between stakeholders → compare against sources and other results (4.3) before specifying anything.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 4.3 (pp.65–66)
Lessing pp.125–128

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



4.3 elements? :: Compare against Source Information; Compare against Other Elicitation Results
Confirm vs verify? :: Confirm = captured information accurate and consistent (4.3); verify = requirement quality (7.2)

Business Analysis Information (communicated)
Information Management Approach


Your discovery findings are solid. Now you have to land them with a COO who wants one page, a store head who hates slide decks, and vendors who need detail. 4.4 Communicate BA Information.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the elements of 4.4
Choose format by audience (formal, informal, presentation)
Recognize communication as bi-directional and iterative



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Communicate BA Information


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Communicate Business Analysis Information so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Make sure stakeholders share the same understanding of business analysis information, using the right format and channel for each audience.
Elements: Determine Objectives and Format of Communication (formal documentation, informal documentation, presentations), and Communicate Business Analysis Package.
Package: prepare, review and approve. Delivery via group collaboration, individual collaboration, or e-mail and other non-verbal methods.
Inputs: Business Analysis Information, Stakeholder Engagement Approach. Guidelines: BA Approach, Information Management Approach. Output: Business Analysis Information (communicated).
Communication is bi-directional: check understanding, don’t just transmit.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

For Marcus (distrusts slides, prefers face-to-face), what format and delivery would you choose?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: informal documentation or a short walkthrough, delivered through individual collaboration face-to-face, per his communication needs from 3.2.



Apply it at GreenBasket: One finding set, three packages
Package your confirmed discovery findings for three audiences.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim workspace/22-elicitation-results-confirmed.md, workspace/11-stakeholder-engagement-approach.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn

Survey or Questionnaire
Observation
Brainstorming
Prototyping

“Which technique should the BA use?” is one of the most common exam question types. Today you learn the selection logic, the strengths and limitations that decide between look-alike techniques.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Select elicitation techniques by situation
Know key strengths and limitations of each
Design a workshop and a survey



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Selection logic


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Workshops, Focus Groups, Survey or Questionnaire so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Workshops: a structured, facilitated event to reach decisions or consensus; roles are sponsor, facilitator, scribe, timekeeper and participants. Can be dominated by strong voices.
Focus groups: 6–12 pre-qualified participants with a moderator; qualitative opinions and attitudes. Not for decisions or consensus.
Surveys: many or dispersed respondents, quick and cheap; closed questions for statistics, open questions for depth. Low response rate and no follow-up probing.
Observation: tacit knowledge and real workflow; people may behave differently when watched.
Brainstorming: many ideas fast, no evaluation during generation. Prototyping: elicit and validate via a model (throw-away vs evolutionary; by purpose: proof of concept, form study, usability, visual).
Benchmarking and market analysis: compare with best practice and competitors. Interface analysis: for each interface, what information crosses it, how, how often, why, and who owns it.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

You need opinions from 400 Basket Rewards members in 3 states within a week. Technique?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: survey or questionnaire: many respondents, geographically dispersed, time-boxed.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Design Workshop #2 (the one that works)
Workshop #1 had no owners, the sponsor left after 30 minutes, and marketing felt shut down.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 10-workshop-notes-raw, Workshops. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Design Workshop #2 on “substitutions and pickup experience”: objective, participants, roles, agenda with timings, techniques inside the workshop (e.g. brainstorming, dot voting, collaborative game), ground rules, and expected outputs. Also write 5 survey questions to test substitution preferences with members.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach it and save the design. Check: a neutral facilitator (not the BA if the BA needs to contribute), decisions captured with owners, Kim and Rosa included, and the customer voice brought in (survey data or personas). Save the result to workspace/25-workshop-2-and-survey-design.md and link it: workspace/25-workshop-2-and-survey-design.md.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

12 CBAP-style questions on: choosing elicitation techniques in scenarios; strengths and limitations of interviews, workshops, focus groups, surveys, observation, brainstorming, prototyping, document analysis, benchmarking, interface analysis.
Build distractors from these traps: focus group for decisions; workshop for large dispersed groups; observation when behaviour is cognitive and not visible; prototype type mix-ups (throw-away vs evolutionary).
Log to scores.csv with ka=TECH and topic=elicitation-techniques.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Decision or consensus → workshop; opinions → focus group; many or dispersed → survey; tacit → observation.
Know one strength and one limitation per technique.


Exam rule of thumb: Read the scenario constraints (group size, geography, time, decision vs opinion). They pick the technique for you.

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Requirements Life Cycle Management
Trace Requirements
Requirements (traced)
Requirements
Designs


Harvest’s post-mortem: “Nobody could tell why a feature existed.” Traceability is the cure. This week is RLCM (15%): managing requirements and designs from inception to retirement. First, 5.1 Trace Requirements.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain RLCM’s scope (inception to retirement) and its 5 tasks
Know the traceability relationships
Build a traceability chain for GreenBasket



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: RLCM at a glance


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Requirements Life Cycle Management so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Five tasks: 5.1 Trace, 5.2 Maintain, 5.3 Prioritize, 5.4 Assess Requirements Changes, 5.5 Approve.
The life cycle starts with the representation of a need and ends when the solution and its requirements are retired, not when the project ends.
RLCM applies to requirements and designs. Outputs come in pairs: Requirements (traced) and Designs (traced), and so on.
Guidelines come from BAPM (Information Management Approach, Governance Approach) and SA/RADD (Change Strategy, Solution Scope, Requirements Architecture).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

When does the requirements life cycle end?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: when the solution and the requirements that represent it are retired. Requirements keep providing value while the solution is in use.



Part 2: Trace Requirements


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Trace Requirements so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Link requirements and designs across levels so that alignment, coverage and the impact of changes are visible.
Elements: Level of Formality, Relationships, Traceability Repository.
Relationships: Derive (a child derived from a parent, e.g. solution from business requirement), Depends (Necessity: only makes sense if the other exists; Effort: easier if the other is implemented), Satisfy (implementation element to the requirement it satisfies), Validate (requirement to the test case that verifies it).
Supports impact analysis, coverage (nothing missing, nothing extra) and scope control.
Inputs: Requirements, Designs. Guidelines: Domain Knowledge, Information Management Approach, Legal/Regulatory Information, Requirements Management Tools/Repository. Outputs: Requirements (traced), Designs (traced).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

“Allergen display on product pages” only makes sense if “product master data includes allergens” exists. Which relationship?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: depends, necessity type.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Traceability formality should match the value and risk. Tracing everything at maximum detail is not the BABOK answer.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Traceability chain for Click & Collect
Show Elena why each feature exists and expose orphans.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 11-draft-requirements-v0, workspace/02-requirements-classification.md, 01-sponsor-kickoff-email. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Build a traceability matrix from 2 business objectives (e.g. reach 5% online share; order accuracy ≥97%) → stakeholder requirements → solution requirements (use R-IDs) → a test idea. Label each link as derive, depends, satisfy or validate. Which requirements trace to no objective?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save the matrix plus a Mermaid trace graph. List orphans (e.g. R-11 recipes, R-03 React Native) and what to do with them: park, challenge, or find their objective. Save the result to workspace/30-traceability-matrix.md and link it: workspace/30-traceability-matrix.md.




                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

R-11 (recipes) traces to no business objective. Traceability just gave you a neutral, evidence-based way to push back on Lily.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

8 CBAP-style questions on: RLCM scope and 5.1 Trace Requirements: relationships (derive, depends necessity/effort, satisfy, validate), formality, uses of traceability.
Build distractors from these traps: life cycle ends at project close; satisfy vs validate relationship; necessity vs effort dependency; trace everything at maximum formality.
Log to scores.csv with ka=RLCM and topic=5.1.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

RLCM runs until retirement and covers requirements and designs.
Relationships: derive, depends (necessity, effort), satisfy, validate.
Traceability supports impact analysis, coverage and scope control.


Exam rule of thumb: A requirement tracing to no business objective is a scope-creep candidate. Challenge it.

Module 4 · Week 5 · ~85 min in session + ~20 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Prioritize Requirements
Prioritization
Decision Analysis
Backlog Management
Requirements (prioritized)
Governance Approach


Tom’s list has 13 “High” priorities, many from one person. Workshop #1’s dot vote said accuracy beats recipes 14 to 1. Today you prioritize properly: 5.3 Prioritize Requirements.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 8 bases for prioritization
Handle the challenges (non-negotiable demands, unrealistic trade-offs)
Apply MoSCoW, ranking and time-boxing



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Prioritize Requirements


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Prioritize Requirements, Prioritization so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Rank requirements and designs by relative importance, with stakeholders, and keep doing so as things change.
Elements: Basis for Prioritization, Challenges of Prioritization, Continual Prioritization.
Basis: benefit, penalty, cost, risk, dependencies, time sensitivity, stability, regulatory or policy compliance.
Challenges: stakeholders may deem everything high priority, try to avoid difficult trade-offs, or the solution team may influence results by exaggerating effort.
Prioritization is continual. The basis can change as context changes.
Technique families: grouping (MoSCoW, high/med/low), ranking, time boxing/budgeting, negotiation.
Inputs: Requirements, Designs. Guidelines include Governance Approach, Change Strategy, Solution Scope, Requirements Architecture, Business Constraints, Domain Knowledge. Outputs: Requirements (prioritized), Designs (prioritized).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

R-19 (hosted payment page) is not exciting for customers, but it is mandatory. Which basis makes it top priority?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: regulatory or policy compliance, with penalty as a secondary basis (the consequence of not doing it).




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Penalty (the consequence of NOT implementing) is a distinct basis from benefit.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Prioritize release 1 (6 pilot stores)
Run the prioritization you would facilitate with Elena, Marcus, Anil, Janet and Lily.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 11-draft-requirements-v0, 10-workshop-notes-raw, 04-customer-feedback-q2, workspace/12-governance-approach.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Apply MoSCoW to R-01..R-20 for release 1. For each Must and each Won’t, name the basis (benefit, penalty, cost, risk, dependencies, time sensitivity, stability, compliance). How will you handle Lily’s “everything is High” and the one-lap rule?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save the prioritized list with the rationale. Must: payment page (compliance), substitution preferences (benefit, accuracy), pick path sorted (benefit), temperature control (compliance), loyalty points (benefit, time). Won’t this time: recipes (no objective), same-day delivery. Coupons are Could or Should depending on cost and the dependency on the loyalty API. Record the dependency R-12 → product master data. Save the result to workspace/32-prioritized-requirements-r1.md and link it: workspace/32-prioritized-requirements-r1.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type elena-sponsor, giving it the path workspace/32-prioritized-requirements-r1.md and ask whether she accepts what is Won’t for release 1. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 5.3 bases, challenges, continual prioritization, prioritization techniques (MoSCoW, ranking, time boxing, negotiation), decision analysis support.
Build distractors from these traps: priority set once; benefit vs penalty; BA decides priority alone; prioritization approach (3.3) vs prioritizing (5.3).
Log to scores.csv with ka=RLCM and topic=5.3.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

8 bases: benefit, penalty, cost, risk, dependencies, time sensitivity, stability, compliance.
Stakeholders decide priorities; the BA facilitates.
Continual: re-prioritize as the context changes.


Exam rule of thumb: The BA facilitates prioritization with stakeholders. An answer where the BA sets priorities alone is wrong.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 5.3 (pp.86–90) and 10.33
Jonasson 5.18 (pp.122–126): dollar, forced-pair, density dotting, AHP



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



Bases for prioritization? :: Benefit, penalty, cost, risk, dependencies, time sensitivity, stability, regulatory/policy compliance
Prioritization technique families? :: Grouping (e.g. MoSCoW), ranking, time boxing/budgeting, negotiation



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (4.3) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 85, set current to 4.4, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 4.4: 5.4 Assess Requirements Changes: CR-017 same-day delivery. Marketing wants delivery in release 1, with media already booked.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready for 4.4? Type /next (or /start 4.4) whenever you are. Short break first is a good idea.

 Student named bases for key items
 Drill logged; task card added

Module 4 · Week 5 · ~85 min in session + ~20 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Assess Requirements Changes
Requirements Change Assessment
Proposed Change
Financial Analysis
12-change-request-CR-017


CR-017 just landed: add same-day delivery to the pilot. +9 weeks, +$640k, alcohol delivery prohibited in State C, and a survey slide that hides the 9% “delivery only” figure. Elena wants a recommendation by Friday. 5.4 Assess Requirements Changes.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 3 elements of 5.4 and the impact analysis factors
Assess a change against the governance approach and change strategy
Write an impact assessment and recommendation



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Assess Requirements Changes


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Assess Requirements Changes so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Work out what a proposed change to requirements or designs would mean (benefit, cost, impact, schedule, urgency) and resolve it through governance.
Elements: Assessment Formality (per governance approach, predictive vs adaptive), Impact Analysis, Impact Resolution.
Impact analysis considers: benefit, cost, impact (on customers, business, solution), schedule, urgency.
Impact resolution: approve, modify, or reject (or defer), per the Governance Approach decision rights, with the outcome communicated and recorded.
Inputs: Proposed Change, Requirements, Designs. Guidelines: Change Strategy, Domain Knowledge, Governance Approach, Legal/Regulatory Information, Requirements Architecture, Solution Scope. Outputs: Requirements Change Assessment, Designs Change Assessment.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Who decides whether CR-017 is accepted: you, Tom, or someone else?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: whoever the Governance Approach (3.3) names, e.g. the change control board chaired by Elena. The BA assesses and recommends.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

The BA does not approve or reject changes unilaterally.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Impact assessment of CR-017
Assess the change honestly. The data is incomplete and presented selectively.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 12-change-request-CR-017, 04-customer-feedback-q2, 08-compliance-memo, 02-harvest-postmortem, workspace/30-traceability-matrix.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Write the impact analysis: benefit (use the full survey data), cost, impact (customers, stores, compliance, solution), schedule, urgency. Which requirements are affected (use traceability)? Then give a recommendation with options (e.g. reject for R1 and defer to R2 with a demand test; modify: pilot delivery in 1 store later; approve with a new date).




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save a Requirements Change Assessment with an options table and a clear recommendation for the change control board. Flag the misleading “47% either” framing (only 9% need delivery) and the State C alcohol prohibition. Save the result to workspace/33-cr-017-change-assessment.md and link it: workspace/33-cr-017-change-assessment.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type elena-sponsor, giving it the path workspace/33-cr-017-change-assessment.md and present the recommendation for decision. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]


                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

Harvest died partly of delivery complexity. The traceability matrix plus impact analysis gives you an evidence-based “not now”, not a political one.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 5.4 elements, impact analysis factors, impact resolution, role of governance, formality in predictive vs adaptive.
Build distractors from these traps: BA approves the change; implement then assess; change assessment vs change strategy; skip assessment for urgent changes.
Log to scores.csv with ka=RLCM and topic=5.4.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Assess formality, analyze impact (benefit, cost, impact, schedule, urgency), resolve per governance.
Traceability makes impact analysis possible.
The BA recommends; the decision makers decide.


Exam rule of thumb: Urgent change requests still go through impact analysis and the agreed change control process.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 5.4 (pp.91–94)
Lessing pp.167–171
Jonasson 6.3.4 (p.138)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



5.4 elements? :: Assessment Formality; Impact Analysis; Impact Resolution
Impact analysis considers? :: Benefit, cost, impact, schedule, urgency
5.4 outputs? :: Requirements Change Assessment; Designs Change Assessment



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (4.4) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 85, set current to 4.5, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 4.5: 5.5 Approve Requirements. Consensus, conflict and sign-off, without a Harvest-style rubber stamp.


                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready for 4.5? Type /next (or /start 4.5) whenever you are. Short break first is a good idea.

Module 4 · Week 5 · ~70 min in session + ~20 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Approve Requirements
Requirements (approved)
Requirements (verified)
Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria


In Harvest, requirements were “signed off” by a delegate while stores never saw them. Now Marcus and Lily disagree on substitutions, and Janet must approve compliance items. 5.5 Approve Requirements.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 4 elements of 5.5
Handle conflict and gain consensus
Know that approval takes Requirements (verified)



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Approve Requirements


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Approve Requirements so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Reach agreement and approval on requirements and designs so that work can continue.
Elements: Understand Stakeholder Roles (who has authority), Conflict and Issue Management, Gain Consensus, Track and Communicate Approval.
Inputs: Requirements (verified), Designs. Guidelines: Change Strategy, Governance Approach, Legal/Regulatory Information, Requirements Management Tools/Repository, Solution Scope. Outputs: Requirements (approved), Designs (approved).
Approval can be formal sign-off (predictive) or ongoing acceptance, e.g. in backlog reviews (adaptive).
Techniques: acceptance and evaluation criteria, decision analysis, item tracking, reviews, workshops.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Marcus (store ops) and Lily (marketing) disagree about per-item substitutions. What does the BA do under “Conflict and Issue Management”?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: facilitate communication, use evidence (survey: accuracy 82% top factor; the oat milk complaint) and decision analysis, track the issue, and escalate to the decision maker defined in governance if unresolved.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Approval plan for release 1 requirements
Make approval real this time.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim workspace/12-governance-approach.md, workspace/32-prioritized-requirements-r1.md, workspace/11-stakeholder-engagement-approach.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Create an approval plan: requirement groups → approver (authority) → reviewers → approval method (formal sign-off vs backlog acceptance) → evidence of verification. Then write how you’ll resolve the substitution conflict and how approvals will be tracked and communicated.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save. Ensure: Janet approves compliance items; Marcus approves store process items (with Rosa and Kim reviewing); Elena approves scope; approvals are recorded in the repository with date and version; the conflict is resolved with a decision-analysis table and evidence. Save the result to workspace/34-approval-plan-r1.md and link it: workspace/34-approval-plan-r1.md.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 5.5 elements, approval inputs (verified), consensus and conflict handling, formal vs adaptive approval, tracking approvals.
Build distractors from these traps: validated as approval input; approval only by sponsor; conflict escalated before facilitation; approval = sign-off only (no adaptive form).
Log to scores.csv with ka=RLCM and topic=5.5.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Approve takes verified requirements.
Know who has authority, manage conflict, gain consensus, track and communicate.
Approval can be formal or continuous (adaptive).


Exam rule of thumb: Conflict at approval → the BA facilitates resolution with evidence first, and escalates per governance only if needed.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 5.5 (pp.95–98)
Lessing pp.171–184 (incl. knowledge quiz)
Jonasson 6.3.5 (p.138)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



5.5 elements? :: Understand Stakeholder Roles; Conflict & Issue Management; Gain Consensus; Track & Communicate Approval
5.5 input requirement state? :: Requirements (verified)



                  
                  What the instructor does

Module 4 · Week 5 · ~75 min in session + ~15 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Decision Analysis
Backlog Management
Business Rules Analysis
Prioritization


Three techniques that show up in RLCM questions and far beyond: decision analysis, backlog management and business rules analysis.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Build a weighted decision matrix
Explain how a backlog is managed
Separate definitional and behavioural business rules



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Decision analysis and backlog management


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Decision Analysis, Backlog Management so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Decision analysis: frame the problem, alternatives, criteria and weights, and uncertainty. Tools: decision matrices (weighted), decision trees (expected value = probability × outcome), pros and cons, trade-offs.
Backlog management: items are prioritized; higher-priority items are elaborated in more detail; the backlog is refined continually; items leave it when implemented or removed.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Option A: a 60% chance of +$500k and a 40% chance of −$100k. What is the expected value?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: 0.6×500 − 0.4×100 = 300 − 40 = $260k.



Part 2: Business rules analysis


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Business Rules Analysis so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Definitional rules: shape concepts and knowledge; they can’t be violated, only misapplied (e.g. “an order is collectable when all items are picked and staged”).
Behavioural rules: shape conduct; they can be violated, so a response is needed (e.g. “alcohol must not be handed to anyone without verified ID”).
Rules are separated from processes so they can change independently. Express them atomically, in business vocabulary, with a single owner.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Classify: “Staff under 18 must not hand over alcohol.” Definitional or behavioural?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: behavioural: it can be violated, so enforcement or response is needed (the pilot logged 2 attempts).



Apply it at GreenBasket: Substitution policy decision + rulebook
Resolve the substitution debate with a decision matrix and capture the rules.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 10-workshop-notes-raw, 04-customer-feedback-q2, 06-competitor-benchmark, 08-compliance-memo. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Build a weighted decision matrix for substitution options (per-order allow/deny; per-item preference; per-item plus live chat) using 4–5 weighted criteria. Then write 6 business rules (substitutions and alcohol), each tagged definitional or behavioural.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach it and check the weights sum to 100% and that rules are atomic. Save both. Save the result to workspace/35-substitution-decision-and-rules.md and link it: workspace/35-substitution-decision-and-rules.md.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: decision analysis (matrices, expected value, trees), backlog management, business rules analysis (definitional vs behavioural), prioritization techniques.
Build distractors from these traps: definitional vs behavioural; business rules embedded in process models; backlog items all equally detailed; decision analysis vs decision modelling.
Log to scores.csv with ka=TECH and topic=rlcm-techniques.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Decision matrices weight criteria; decision trees use expected value.
Backlog: prioritized, progressively elaborated, continually refined.
Definitional rules can’t be violated; behavioural rules can.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 10.2, 10.9, 10.16



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



Definitional vs behavioural rule? :: Definitional shapes knowledge (can’t be violated); behavioural shapes conduct (can be violated)
Expected value? :: Sum of (probability × outcome)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Update progress/progress.json: add this lesson (4.6) to completed with today’s date and minutes ≈ 75, set current to 4.7, and update weak_topics if the drill exposed any.


Next up: Lesson 4.7: RLCM exam drill (40 questions). Prove RLCM mastery.


                  
                  Your turn
