Module 5 · Week 6 · ~80 min in session + ~20 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Strategy Analysis
Analyze Current State
Current State Description
Business Requirements
Root Cause Analysis
SWOT Analysis


David Chen, the CFO, won’t fund anything until you can explain why GreenBasket must change, in evidence, not adjectives. Strategy Analysis (15%) starts with 6.1 Analyze Current State, the most technique-heavy task in the BABOK (26 techniques).
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Explain SA’s 4 tasks and flow
Know the 8 elements of 6.1 and its two outputs
Use root cause analysis and SWOT on real data



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: SA at a glance


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Strategy Analysis so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Four tasks: 6.1 Analyze Current State → 6.2 Define Future State → 6.3 Assess Risks → 6.4 Define Change Strategy.
SA can happen before, during or after a project. It covers the need, the context, and the strategy to get from current to future state.
SA outputs guide RADD and SE: Business Objectives, Future State Description, Potential Value, Risk Analysis Results, Change Strategy, Solution Scope.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Put the 4 SA tasks in their logical order.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: current → future → risks → change strategy (and it iterates).



Part 2: Analyze Current State


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Analyze Current State so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Understand why the enterprise needs to change and what the change would affect, starting from how things work today.
Elements: Business Needs, Organizational Structure and Culture, Capabilities and Processes, Technology and Infrastructure, Policies, Business Architecture, Internal Assets, External Influencers (industry structure, competitors, customers, suppliers, political and regulatory, technology, macroeconomic).
Business needs can come from the top down, bottom up, middle management, or external drivers. Understand the problem or opportunity, not just the symptom.
Inputs: Elicitation Results, Needs. Outputs: Current State Description and Business Requirements.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which task outputs Business Requirements?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: 6.1, together with the Current State Description.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Business Requirements do NOT come from Define Future State.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Current State Description + Business Requirements
Build the “why change” case from evidence.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 05-market-and-sales-data, 04-customer-feedback-q2, 06-competitor-benchmark, 07-it-landscape, workspace/22-elicitation-results-confirmed.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Draft (1) a fishbone or 5-whys for “visit frequency down 11%”, (2) a SWOT, and (3) a current-state summary using the 8 elements (one line each). Then write 3 business requirements (goals and outcomes) that follow from it.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach, check SWOT internal/external placement, and save the Current State Description with its business requirements. Include a small table computed from the CSV (share trend, visit frequency trend, competitor online share). Save the result to workspace/40-current-state-description.md and link it: workspace/40-current-state-description.md.




                  
                  Model answer (try it yourself first) 
                  
                


Root causes: no online channel (convenience gap), competitor online share 4.1→11.2%, low digital capability, inventory accuracy 82%
SWOT: S = loyal members (410k), store footprint, trusted brand; W = no e-commerce, legacy stock system, data quality; O = 71% would use C&C, pickup preference 44%; T = FreshWay/QuickCart, union constraints (external? internal HR policy vs external law: discuss)
Business requirements: stop share decline; restore visit frequency; achieve an online channel reaching 5% of sales within 2 years of launch





                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type cbap-examiner, giving it the path workspace/40-current-state-description.md and check the 8 elements and SWOT placement. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: SA overview and 6.1 elements, business need sources, outputs, root cause analysis, SWOT.
Build distractors from these traps: business requirements from 6.2; SWOT threats as internal; symptom treated as root cause; SA only before projects.
Log to scores.csv with ka=SA and topic=6.1.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

6.1 answers “why change?” with 8 elements.
Outputs: Current State Description AND Business Requirements.
Find root causes, not symptoms.


Exam rule of thumb: When a stakeholder describes a symptom, the BA first investigates the root cause and the business need.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 6.0–6.1 (pp.99–109)
Lessing ch.9 pp.185–198
Jonasson 7.3.1 (pp.145–150) and 7.6 (p.159)

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



6.1 outputs? :: Current State Description; Business Requirements
6.1 elements? :: Business Needs; Org Structure & Culture; Capabilities & Processes; Technology & Infrastructure; Policies; Business Architecture; Internal Assets; External Influencers
SWOT internal vs external? :: Strengths/Weaknesses internal; Opportunities/Threats external

By the end of this session you will be able to:

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Define Future State


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Define Future State so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Describe the target conditions that would satisfy the business need, including measurable objectives and the value expected.
Elements: Business Goals and Objectives, Scope of Solution Space, Constraints, Organizational Structure and Culture, Capabilities and Processes, Technology and Infrastructure, Policies, Business Architecture, Internal Assets, Identify Assumptions, Potential Value.
Goals: long-term, ongoing, qualitative. Objectives: measurable, SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bounded).
Constraints: budget, time, technology, policies, regulation… Assumptions must be identified because they carry risk.
Input: Business Requirements. Outputs: Business Objectives, Future State Description, Potential Value.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Make “improve pickup experience” SMART.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: e.g. “95% of pickups completed within 5 minutes of customer arrival across pilot stores by week 10 of the pilot”.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Goals vs objectives: the measurable one is the objective.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Future State Description

                  What the instructor does

                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save. Check SMARTness, and that “real-time stock” becomes a feasible future state (near-real-time plus stock confidence plus inventory accuracy improvement). Assumptions such as “loyalty API supports coupons” should be flagged as false (it doesn’t). Save the result to workspace/41-future-state-description.md and link it: workspace/41-future-state-description.md.

Future state: dedicated picker roles funded centrally, staging with temperature control, inventory accuracy ≥95% in pilot stores, pickup bays where space allows
Constraints: $3.2M budget, 6-month pilot, union 45-day consultation, PCI, alcohol rules

Goals are qualitative; objectives are SMART.
11 elements; the future state covers people, process, technology and policy.

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Assess Risks
Risk Analysis Results
Risk Analysis and Management


Inventory accuracy of 74% in fresh. A union consultation that nobody has started. A security review that could add 8 weeks. 6.3 Assess Risks makes these visible before the change strategy is chosen.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 5 elements of 6.3
Build a risk register with likelihood, impact and responses
Explain risk tolerance (averse, neutral, seeking)



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Assess Risks


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Assess Risks, Risk Analysis and Management so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Identify and weigh the uncertainties that could reduce value during the transition or in the future state, and recommend how to proceed.
Elements: Unknowns; Constraints, Assumptions and Dependencies; Negative Impact to Value; Risk Tolerance (risk-aversion, neutrality, risk-seeking); Recommendation.
Recommendation: pursue the benefits regardless of risk, pursue while investing in reducing risk, seek ways to increase benefits to outweigh risk, find ways to realize benefits while reducing risk, or do not pursue.
Risk responses (technique): avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, and for opportunities increase. Risk level = likelihood × impact.
Inputs: Business Objectives, Elicitation Results (confirmed), Influences, Potential Value, Requirements (prioritized). Output: Risk Analysis Results.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Buying insurance or contracting the courier to carry delivery liability is which response?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: transfer (sharing): moving the impact to a third party.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Assess the risks of not changing too. Doing nothing has risks (continued share loss).



Apply it at GreenBasket: Risk register and recommendation
Give Elena and David an honest risk picture.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 07-it-landscape, 08-compliance-memo, 02-harvest-postmortem, workspace/41-future-state-description.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Build a risk register of at least 8 risks (including one risk of NOT changing): cause → risk → consequence, likelihood (1–5), impact (1–5), score, response type, owner. What is the organization’s risk tolerance, and what’s your recommendation?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save with a heat-map table. Key risks: inventory data quality (mitigate: cycle counts and a stock-confidence indicator); union consultation delay (mitigate: start now); security review adds 6–8 weeks (mitigate: start in parallel); store adoption (mitigate: central picker funding, pilot store choice); vendor lock-in; alcohol compliance incident; handheld failure; risk of not changing (share keeps falling). Save the result to workspace/42-risk-analysis-results.md and link it: workspace/42-risk-analysis-results.md.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 6.3 elements, risk tolerance types, recommendation options, risk responses, inputs and output.
Build distractors from these traps: ignore risk of not changing; transfer vs mitigate; Risk Analysis Results produced by 6.4; risk-neutral vs risk-seeking.
Log to scores.csv with ka=SA and topic=6.3.

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

5 elements, ending in a recommendation.
Risk tolerance: averse, neutral, seeking.
Consider the risk of doing nothing.

BABOK 6.3 (pp.120–123), 10.38
Jonasson 4.5.1 (pp.64–67) and 7.4 (p.157)

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Define Change Strategy
Change Strategy
Solution Scope
Business Cases
Scope Modelling


Current state: done. Future state: done. Risks: done. Now: how do we get there? 6.4 Define Change Strategy produces the two outputs that frame everything in RADD: the Change Strategy and the Solution Scope.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 5 elements of 6.4
Perform gap analysis and an enterprise readiness assessment
Define transition states and release planning
Include “do nothing” and opportunity cost in the alternatives



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Define Change Strategy


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Define Change Strategy so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Compare ways of getting from the current to the future state, pick one, and define the solution scope and transition path.
Elements: Solution Scope, Gap Analysis, Enterprise Readiness Assessment, Change Strategy (alternatives including do nothing, opportunity cost, investment, timeline), Transition States and Release Planning.
Opportunity cost: the benefits forgone by choosing one alternative over another.
Inputs: Current State Description, Future State Description, Risk Analysis Results, Stakeholder Engagement Approach. Outputs: Change Strategy and Solution Scope.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

What’s the difference between the Change Strategy and the Solution Scope?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: Change Strategy = the approach to move from current to future state (transition states, releases, readiness). Solution Scope = the boundaries of the solution (capabilities in and out).




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Both are outputs of 6.4. Distractors credit Solution Scope to RADD.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Change strategy for Click & Collect
Compare real alternatives and design the path.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim workspace/40-current-state-description.md, workspace/41-future-state-description.md, workspace/42-risk-analysis-results.md, 13-vendor-proposals. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Produce: (1) a gap analysis (current → future per capability), (2) an enterprise readiness assessment (cultural, operational, technical), (3) 3 change strategy alternatives including “do nothing”, with opportunity cost, (4) transition states (e.g. data-fix → 6-store pilot → wave rollout), and (5) the solution scope (in and out, incl. delivery and recipes).




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save with a scope model (context diagram in Mermaid) and a transition roadmap. Readiness gaps: store incentives, union, inventory accuracy, handhelds. Save the result to workspace/43-change-strategy-and-solution-scope.md and link it: workspace/43-change-strategy-and-solution-scope.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type marcus-store-ops, giving it the path workspace/43-change-strategy-and-solution-scope.md and ask whether the readiness assessment and transition states are realistic for stores. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]


                  
                  Discovery 
                  
                

The readiness assessment predicts the exact problems the pilot will show in week 9 (incentives, aisle data). Keep this file. You’ll compare it with the real results.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 6.4 elements, gap analysis, enterprise readiness, alternatives incl. do nothing and opportunity cost, transition states, outputs.
Build distractors from these traps: Solution Scope from RADD; change strategy = project plan; readiness only technical; no do-nothing option.
Log to scores.csv with ka=SA and topic=6.4.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

6.4 outputs: Change Strategy + Solution Scope.
Readiness is cultural, operational and technical.
Always evaluate “do nothing” and opportunity cost.


Exam rule of thumb: Transition states and release planning belong to the change strategy (6.4), not to RADD.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 6.4 (pp.124–131), 10.41 Scope Modelling
Lessing pp.211–228 (incl. knowledge quiz)
Jonasson 7.3.3–7.3.4 (pp.152–155)

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



6.4 elements? :: Solution Scope; Gap Analysis; Enterprise Readiness Assessment; Change Strategy; Transition States & Release Planning
6.4 outputs? :: Change Strategy; Solution Scope
Opportunity cost? :: The benefits forgone by choosing one alternative over another

Module 5 · Week 6 · ~90 min in session + ~20 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Business Cases
Financial Analysis
Estimation


David Chen: “I need payback within 3 years and a positive NPV, or this doesn’t go to the board.” Today you build the business case and do the calculations the exam expects you to understand.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Structure a business case (need, outcomes, alternatives, recommendation)
Calculate ROI, payback, NPV; interpret IRR
Explain TCO, cost of change and sensitivity analysis



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Business cases


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Business Cases so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Business case sections: Need Assessment, Desired Outcomes, Assess Alternatives (including do nothing: scope, feasibility, assumptions, risks, constraints, financial analysis), Recommended Solution.
A business case is a living document, revisited when the context changes.


Part 2: Financial analysis


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Financial Analysis so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Cost of the change, total cost of ownership (acquire + operate over the life), value realization, cost-benefit analysis.
ROI = (total benefits − total costs) / total costs. Payback period = time until cumulative benefits cover costs (no time value of money).
Present value: future cash discounted, PV = CF / (1 + r)^t. NPV = sum of PVs minus the initial investment. Positive NPV = worth doing at that discount rate.
IRR = the discount rate where NPV = 0. Higher is better, compared against the hurdle rate. Sensitivity analysis tests how results change when assumptions vary.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Investment $1.1M now; net benefits $500k per year for 3 years; discount rate 10%. Rough NPV?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: PV = 500/1.1 + 500/1.21 + 500/1.331 ≈ 454.5 + 413.2 + 375.7 = 1,243.4; NPV ≈ 1,243 − 1,100 = +$143k. Payback ≈ 2.2 years.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Business case: three alternatives + do nothing
Use the vendor proposals and your own assumptions (state them).


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 13-vendor-proposals, 05-market-and-sales-data, workspace/43-change-strategy-and-solution-scope.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Compute a 3-year view for ShelfWise, CodeHarbor and OmniGrocer (one-off + run cost + extra items such as the Connect API, coupons module, security review, pickers), with an assumed benefit ramp (state your assumptions, e.g. online sales margin). Then give ROI, payback and NPV at 10% for each, and a do-nothing line (revenue erosion).




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Do the arithmetic carefully (show a table; you may use a quick Python calculation via Bash to avoid errors), coach interpretation, add a sensitivity check (benefits −30%), and save the business case with the 4 BABOK sections. Save the result to workspace/44-business-case.md and link it: workspace/44-business-case.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type elena-sponsor, giving it the path workspace/44-business-case.md and ask whether this is board-ready and what the CFO will challenge. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: business case structure, ROI, payback, PV/NPV, IRR interpretation, TCO, sensitivity analysis; includes 3 small calculations.
Build distractors from these traps: payback considers time value (it doesn’t); IRR vs NPV meaning; ROI formula inverted; TCO = purchase price only.
Log to scores.csv with ka=TECH and topic=financial-analysis.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Business case = need, outcomes, alternatives (incl. do nothing), recommendation.
NPV > 0 → value-creating at that rate; IRR = rate where NPV = 0.
Payback ignores the time value of money.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 10.7, 10.20 (pp.234–235, 274–278)
Lessing pp.361–363, 384–388
Jonasson 7.3.5, 7.5 (pp.156–158)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



NPV? :: Sum of discounted future cash flows minus initial investment

Welcome to RADD: 30% of the exam, about 36 questions. For two weeks you’ll turn GreenBasket’s confirmed findings into modelled, verified, validated requirements, then recommend a vendor. First: 7.1 Specify and Model Requirements, and the five model categories the exam loves.

Part 1: RADD at a glance


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Requirements Analysis and Design Definition so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Six tasks: 7.1 Specify and Model → 7.2 Verify → 7.3 Validate → 7.4 Define Requirements Architecture → 7.5 Define Design Options → 7.6 Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution.
RADD bridges strategy (SA outputs as guidelines) and delivery. It applies to requirements and designs.
States: specified and modelled → verified / validated → (RLCM) prioritized, approved. 7.5 needs validated, prioritized requirements.

Part 2: Specify and Model Requirements


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Specify and Model Requirements so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Turn elicitation results into structured, modelled requirements and designs at the right level of detail.
Elements: Model Requirements, Analyze Requirements (decomposition, expansion, contraction; identify gaps), Represent Requirements and Attributes, Implement the Appropriate Levels of Abstraction.
Model categories: People and Roles (org models, roles and permissions matrix, stakeholder maps/personas); Rationale (decision models, scope models, business model canvas, root cause, business rules); Activity Flow (process models, use cases and scenarios, user stories); Capability (business capability analysis, functional decomposition, prototypes); Data and Information (data dictionary, data flow diagrams, data models, glossary, state models, interface analysis).
Models can be matrices (tables) or diagrams.
Input: Elicitation Results (any state). 24 techniques. Output: Requirements (specified and modelled).

Part 1: Qualities and interfaces


                  
                  What the instructor does

Key points

NFR categories: availability, compatibility, functionality, maintainability, performance efficiency, portability, reliability, scalability, security, usability, certification, compliance, localization, service level agreements, extensibility. Each needs measures and context.
Acceptance criteria: minimum conditions to accept ONE solution (pass/fail). Evaluation criteria: measures used to rank SEVERAL options.
Prototypes: throw-away vs evolutionary/functional; purposes: proof of principle/concept, form study, usability, visual, functional. Types: storyboards, wireframes, mock-ups, simulations.
Interface analysis: user, system and business interfaces. Identify each one, then pin down what crosses it, how, when, and who owns it.

Alcohol handover is a repeatable decision with rules. Store roles need clear permissions. The whole solution needs decomposing. Today: decision modelling, roles and permissions, functional decomposition, scope modelling.

Part 1: Four structure techniques


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Decision Modelling, Roles and Permissions Matrix, Functional Decomposition so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Decision modelling: decision tables and trees, DMN; separates repeatable business decisions (and their rules) from process flow.
Roles and permissions matrix: roles × activities, with authority levels; supports segregation of duties and security.
Functional decomposition: break outcomes, functions, processes or products into smaller parts until they are manageable. Beware inconsistent decomposition levels.
Scope models: context diagrams, use case diagrams, feature lists; show in/out of scope and boundaries.

Module 6 · Week 7 · ~90 min in session + ~20 min reading
Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Process Modelling
Use Cases and Scenarios
User Stories
Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria
Sequence Diagrams


Kim and Rosa gave you the real picking flow. Today you model it three ways: a process model, a use case, and user stories with acceptance criteria. The exam checks when each is the right choice.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Draw a process model with the right elements
Write a use case with main, alternative and exception flows
Write INVEST user stories with acceptance criteria



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Three views of behaviour


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Process Modelling, Use Cases and Scenarios, User Stories so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Process models: activities, events, directional flow, decision points, links, roles (swimlanes). Notations: flowcharts, activity diagrams, BPMN, value stream maps.
Use cases: actor, goal, preconditions, trigger, main success flow, alternative and exception flows, post-conditions (guarantees). Scenario = one path through a use case.
User stories: “As a , I want , so that ”, plus acceptance criteria; INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable); the 3 Cs (Card, Conversation, Confirmation).
Sequence diagrams show interactions between objects or actors over time (lifelines, messages).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Customer arrives at the store and the order isn’t ready. Main flow, alternative flow, or exception flow of “Collect Order”?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: an exception flow when the goal cannot be completed as planned (or an alternative if the goal is still met another way, e.g. wait under 5 minutes). The key is that both are documented separately from the main success scenario.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Model “Pick & Hand Over Order”
Use the confirmed elicitation results.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim workspace/22-elicitation-results-confirmed.md, workspace/35-substitution-decision-and-rules.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Produce: (1) a swimlane process from order released → picked (by temperature zone) → staged → customer arrives → ID check (alcohol) → handover; (2) a use case “Collect Order” with main, 2 alternative and 2 exception flows; (3) 3 user stories with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria (substitution preference, arrival notification, alcohol handover).




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach it, then save all three. Draw the process in Mermaid (flowchart with subgraphs as lanes). Save the result to workspace/51-pick-handover-models.md and link it: workspace/51-pick-handover-models.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type priyanka-qa, giving it the path workspace/51-pick-handover-models.md and review the acceptance criteria for testability. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: process modelling elements and notations, use case structure, user story format and INVEST, acceptance criteria, sequence diagrams: which to use when.
Build distractors from these traps: use case = user story; process model shows data transformation (that is DFD); acceptance criteria vs evaluation criteria; sequence diagram vs state diagram.
Log to scores.csv with ka=TECH and topic=behaviour-models.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Process model = flow of activities; use case = actor-goal interaction; user story = small valuable slice.
Acceptance criteria make stories testable.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 10.35, 10.42, 10.47, 10.48
Jonasson 8.3.1.1 and 8.3.1.4 (pp.173–197)

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



INVEST? :: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Use case components? :: Actor, goal, preconditions, trigger, main flow, alternative/exception flows, post-conditions

Data Modelling
Data Dictionary
Glossary
Data Flow Diagrams
Concept Modelling
State Modelling


“Order”, “substitution”, “collectable”, “staged”: if stores, marketing and the vendor each define these differently, the pilot fails. Today: the data and information models.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Build a conceptual data model with cardinality
Write data dictionary and glossary entries
Draw a DFD and a state model
Distinguish concept model / data model / glossary / data dictionary



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Data and information models


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Data Modelling, Data Flow Diagrams, State Modelling so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Data models: conceptual, logical, physical. Entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality (e.g. one Order has many Order Lines). ERD or class diagram.
Data dictionary: primitive elements (name, aliases, values/meanings, description) and composite elements (sequence, repetition, optional).
Glossary: business terms and definitions. Concept model: business vocabulary (noun and verb concepts), independent of data design.
DFD: external entities, processes, data stores, data flows. Levels: context (level 0), level 1, level 2. No direct flow between external entities or data stores.
State model: entity life cycle as states, transitions and events.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Draw (in words) the states of an Order from placement to completion.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: e.g. Placed → Picking → Picked → Staged → Ready for Collection → Collected; plus Cancelled and Partially Refused (alcohol ID failure) with the triggering events.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Order data and life cycle
Define the data the vendor must support.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 07-it-landscape, 08-compliance-memo, workspace/51-pick-handover-models.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Produce: a conceptual data model (Customer, Order, Order Line, Product, Store, Pickup Slot, Substitution Preference, Tote, Temperature Log, ID Check), 5 glossary terms, 4 data dictionary entries (incl. one composite), a level-0 DFD, and an Order state model.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save with Mermaid (erDiagram and stateDiagram). Note privacy constraints: no ID storage; retention 24 months. Save the result to workspace/52-data-models.md and link it: workspace/52-data-models.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type anil-architect, giving it the path workspace/52-data-models.md and check integration and data feasibility. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: data models, data dictionary (primitive/composite), glossary vs data dictionary, concept model, DFD rules and levels, state models.
Build distractors from these traps: glossary vs data dictionary; concept model vs data model; DFD shows sequence/decisions; direct flow between two data stores.
Log to scores.csv with ka=TECH and topic=data-models.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Glossary = business terms; data dictionary = data elements.
DFD = data movement, not sequence.
State model = life cycle of one entity.

Reading before the next session:

BABOK 10.11–10.15, 10.23, 10.44
Jonasson 8.3.1.2–8.3.1.3 (pp.177–184)



                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Append these flashcards to workspace/flashcards.md (create it if missing; format Q :: A, one per line), then tell the student how many you added:



DFD components? :: External entities, processes, data stores, data flows
Glossary vs data dictionary? :: Glossary defines business terms; data dictionary defines data elements (values, composition)

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Verify Requirements
Requirements (verified)
Reviews
Commonly Confused Concepts
11-draft-requirements-v0


Priyanka says half of Tom’s requirements are untestable. She’s being generous. Today: 7.2 Verify Requirements, the quality check before approval.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Name the 9 characteristics of requirements quality
Run verification activities with checklists
Rewrite flawed requirements



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Verify Requirements


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Verify Requirements so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Check that requirement and design specifications are of good quality and fit for their purpose.
Elements: Characteristics of Requirements and Designs Quality, Verification Activities, Checklists.
Quality characteristics: atomic, complete, consistent, concise, feasible, unambiguous, testable, prioritized, understandable.
Verification activities: check compliance with standards, correct use of modelling notation, completeness within each model, consistency across models, terminology is understood.
Input: Requirements (specified and modelled). Output: Requirements (verified). Techniques: acceptance and evaluation criteria, item tracking, metrics and KPIs, reviews.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

R-06 packs 4 requirements into one sentence. Which characteristic does it violate?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: atomic (and arguably testable and unambiguous for “fast”). Split it into 4.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Verify ≠ validate. “Does it align with business objectives?” is validation (7.3).



Apply it at GreenBasket: Verify and rewrite the draft requirements
Run a verification review on R-01..R-20.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim 11-draft-requirements-v0. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

For at least 10 requirements: name the violated characteristic(s) and rewrite them. Start with R-01, R-02, R-04, R-06, R-07, R-08, R-13/R-14 (conflict!), R-18, R-20.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save a verification log (ID, issue, characteristic, rewrite), plus a reusable checklist. Examples: R-01 “fast and user-friendly” → unambiguous/testable; R-02 real-time stock → feasible; R-13 vs R-14 → consistent; R-18 availability → needs context (hours, measurement window). Save the result to workspace/53-verification-log.md and link it: workspace/53-verification-log.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type priyanka-qa, giving it the path workspace/53-verification-log.md and review the rewrites. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 7.2 quality characteristics, verification activities, checklists, verify vs validate, input and output states.
Build distractors from these traps: verify vs validate; verified vs validated as Approve input; complete vs consistent; feasible vs testable.
Log to scores.csv with ka=RADD and topic=7.2.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

9 characteristics: atomic, complete, consistent, concise, feasible, unambiguous, testable, prioritized, understandable.
Verify = quality of the specification; output Requirements (verified) → 5.5.


Exam rule of thumb: Verify = “built right” (quality). Validate = “right thing” (value and alignment).

Your requirements are now well-formed. But does “recipes and meal plans” help reach 5% online share or 97% accuracy? 7.3 Validate Requirements checks alignment with business value.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 3 elements of 7.3
Define measurable evaluation criteria
Evaluate alignment with the solution scope



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Validate Requirements


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Validate Requirements so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Check that requirements and designs support the business requirements and will deliver the value that is needed.
Elements: Identify Assumptions, Define Measurable Evaluation Criteria, Evaluate Alignment with Solution Scope.
Input: Requirements (specified and modelled). Guidelines: Business Objectives, Future State Description, Potential Value, Solution Scope. Output: Requirements (validated).
A requirement that is valid but outside the solution scope → change the scope or remove the requirement.
Validation is ongoing and involves the customer, end users and sponsor.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

R-11 (recipes) is well-written but supports no business objective. Verify issue or validate issue, and what happens to it?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: validation: it doesn’t align with the objectives or the solution scope. Remove it or move it to a future backlog (a scope change would need governance).



Apply it at GreenBasket: Validation matrix
Validate the verified requirements against objectives and scope.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim workspace/53-verification-log.md, workspace/41-future-state-description.md, workspace/43-change-strategy-and-solution-scope.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

For each verified requirement: which business objective it supports, the assumption it relies on, a measurable evaluation criterion, and in-scope yes/no. Which ones fail validation?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save the validation matrix. Flag failing requirements (recipes, React Native, same-day delivery) and assumptions (e.g. coupons via API is FALSE, so R-10 needs a design option or deferral). Save the result to workspace/54-validation-matrix.md and link it: workspace/54-validation-matrix.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type cbap-examiner, giving it the path workspace/54-validation-matrix.md and check that validation (not verification) logic is used. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 7.3 elements, validation vs verification, evaluation criteria, alignment with solution scope, guidelines used.
Build distractors from these traps: validate = check quality; validated requirements go to Approve; validation only at the end.
Log to scores.csv with ka=RADD and topic=7.3.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Validate = aligns with business requirements and delivers value.
Elements: assumptions, measurable evaluation criteria, alignment with solution scope.
Output: Requirements (validated) → Define Design Options.

BABOK 7.3 (pp.144–147)

Knowledge graph notes for this lesson

Define Requirements Architecture
Requirements Architecture
Information Management Approach


You now have process models, data models, user stories, rules and NFRs. Do they fit together, with no gaps and no contradictions? 7.4 Define Requirements Architecture.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 5 elements of 7.4
Explain viewpoints vs views
Check completeness across views



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Define Requirements Architecture


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Define Requirements Architecture so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Make sure the requirements fit together as a coherent, complete whole that achieves the objectives.
Elements: Requirements Viewpoints and Views, Template Architectures, Completeness, Relate and Verify Requirements Relationships, Business Analysis Information Architecture.
Viewpoint = the conventions for a type of view (model types, notation, stakeholders served). View = an actual set of requirements and models seen from that viewpoint (e.g. “pick process view”).
Relationships to verify: defined, necessary, correct, unambiguous, consistent.
Inputs: Information Management Approach, Requirements (any state), Solution Scope. Output: Requirements Architecture, a guideline for 5.3, 5.4, 7.1 and an input to 7.5.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Is “BPMN process models for store staff” a viewpoint or a view? And “the Riverton picking process model”?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: viewpoint (convention and template); view (a specific instance).




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

7.4 (how requirements fit together) vs 3.4 (how information is stored and managed).



Apply it at GreenBasket: Requirements architecture for release 1
Show how the pieces fit together, and find the gaps.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim workspace/50-model-plan.md, workspace/51-pick-handover-models.md, workspace/52-data-models.md, workspace/54-validation-matrix.md. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Define 4 viewpoints (e.g. customer journey, store operations, data/integration, compliance), map existing views to them, and run a completeness check: what is missing (e.g. NFRs, customer service, refunds, reporting)? Any conflicts across views?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save with a Mermaid diagram of viewpoints → views → requirements, plus a gap list. Save the result to workspace/55-requirements-architecture.md and link it: workspace/55-requirements-architecture.md.



Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 7.4 elements, viewpoints vs views, template architectures, completeness, relationship verification, 3.4 vs 7.4.
Build distractors from these traps: viewpoint vs view; 3.4 vs 7.4; Requirements Architecture as input to Approve.
Log to scores.csv with ka=RADD and topic=7.4.




                  
                  Your turn

Decision day. Elena likes ShelfWise; the evidence may not. 7.6 Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution, where BAs earn their credibility.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Know the 4 elements of 7.6
Weigh expected benefits and costs to determine value

                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Purpose (in our words): Compare the value of each design option and recommend the most suitable one, or none.
Elements: Expected Benefits, Expected Costs (acquisition, operation, opportunity cost…), Determine Value, Assess Design Options and Recommend Solution (considering available resources, constraints, dependencies).
The recommendation may be that no option delivers enough value, so do nothing or re-scope.
Inputs: Potential Value, Design Options. Output: Solution Recommendation.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

What if every option costs more than the value it delivers?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: recommend not proceeding (or re-scoping). It’s a valid BABOK recommendation.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Solution recommendation
Weighted scoring plus value, then a recommendation Elena can take to the board.


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Open and skim workspace/56-design-options.md, workspace/44-business-case.md, 13-vendor-proposals. Share the links and summarize the relevant facts in 3–5 bullets. Don’t solve the exercise.

                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Coach and save. The evidence usually favours OmniGrocer (fit, compliance, references at scale, integration layer) despite a higher one-off cost than ShelfWise. Include the conditions: coupons module decision, inventory-accuracy programme, security review in parallel. Save the result to workspace/57-solution-recommendation.md and link it: workspace/57-solution-recommendation.md.




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Get a stakeholder review. Use the Agent tool with subagent_type elena-sponsor, giving it the path workspace/57-solution-recommendation.md and present the recommendation; she preferred ShelfWise. Relay the review to the student in 3–6 lines.




                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

How would you respond to that feedback? What would you change?


[If the student wants changes, update the workspace file.]

Exam drill


                  
                  Exam drill 
                  
                

10 CBAP-style questions on: 7.6 elements, benefits and costs incl. opportunity cost, determining value, recommendation options incl. none.

Log to scores.csv with ka=RADD and topic=7.6.

Before we wrap up, which question felt shakiest, and why?

Re-explain that concept in a different way (analogy or GreenBasket example) in 3–4 lines.



Wrap-up
Key takeaways:

Value = expected benefits − expected costs (incl. opportunity cost), in context.
Recommending “none” is legitimate.
Output: Solution Recommendation.


Exam rule of thumb: The BA recommends the option with the best value for the need, not the sponsor’s favourite or the cheapest.

Key points

SE questions often hinge on measurement techniques. Today: metrics and KPIs (indicator vs metric vs KPI), data mining (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive), vendor assessment, and root cause analysis revisited.

Part 1: Measurement toolkit


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Metrics and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), Data Mining, Vendor Assessment so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Indicator: a specific numerical measure of progress. Metric: a quantifiable level of an indicator, e.g. a target. KPI: an indicator of progress towards a strategic goal. Good indicators are clear, relevant, economical, adequate and quantifiable. Consider the data source, collection method and reporting.
Data mining: descriptive (patterns, clustering), diagnostic (why: decision trees, association), predictive (forecast). Supports decision making; needs quality data.
Vendor assessment: knowledge and expertise, licensing and pricing models, product or vendor market position, terms and conditions, experience, reputation and stability.
Root cause analysis: fishbone (Ishikawa) categories, five whys.

                  What the instructor does

The analytical toolkit: how BAs decide, quantify and control. These show up across nearly every KA.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Compare analytical and decision techniques
Recall key formulas and lists (PERT, NPV, risk responses, bases of prioritization)



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: Toolkit review
Key points

Decision analysis (alternatives under uncertainty) vs decision modelling (repeatable decisions) vs business rules analysis (individual rules).
Risk: likelihood × impact; avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, increase. Financial: ROI, payback, NPV, IRR, TCO. Estimation: PERT (O+4M+P)/6, Delphi, analogous, bottom-up, top-down, rolling wave, parametric.
Prioritization: grouping, ranking, time boxing/budgeting, negotiation. Backlog: prioritized, progressively elaborated.
Glossary (terms) vs data dictionary (data elements). Acceptance (one, pass/fail) vs evaluation (rank many). Item tracking (issues to closure).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Three-point estimate: O=4, M=6, P=14 days. PERT?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: (4 + 24 + 14) / 6 = 7.



Apply it at GreenBasket: Master technique sheet, part 3

Commonly Confused Concepts
progress/error-log.md


You know the content. Now we train the test-taking: how to read a long case, eliminate options, and manage 210 minutes without panic.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

Apply a 4-step question method
Use elimination on “all plausible” options
Plan pacing checkpoints



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Ready to dive in?



Part 1: The 4-step method
Key points



Read the last sentence first: what is asked (task? technique? output? next step? FIRST/BEST/NOT?).




Identify the context: which KA and task is happening, which perspective (agile? BI?), and which state the information is in (unconfirmed? verified?).




Eliminate: out-of-role actions (BA approves alone, PM duties), wrong state labels, real-life-but-not-BABOK answers, absolute words (always/never).




Choose the answer that follows the task’s purpose, involves the right stakeholders, and serves value.


Pacing: 120 questions / 210 min. Checkpoints: Q40 at about 65 min, Q80 at about 135 min, Q120 at about 195 min, leaving 15 min to review flags.



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Why read the last sentence first on a long case study?




                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Give feedback. A strong answer includes: it tells you what to extract from the scenario, which saves re-reading.



Part 2: Classic distractor patterns


                  
                  What the instructor does 
                  
                

Re-read Commonly Confused Concepts so every name you use is BABOK-exact. Share the link(s) with the student.


Key points

Right concept, wrong state (“validated” vs “verified”).
Right action, wrong owner (BA decides priorities or approves changes).
Right action, wrong timing (escalate before trying collaboration; build before assessing).
Real-world shortcut vs BABOK practice (skip confirmation because the sponsor is in a hurry).
Plan vs perform confusion (3.3 plans prioritization; 5.3 performs it).



                  
                  Your turn 
                  
                

Which of those patterns caught you most often in your error log?



Exam drill

Last sentence first, context second, eliminate third, value fourth.

index.title: CBAP in 13 Weeks
index.content:
A free, interactive path to the IIBA® CBAP® exam. Study 10 hours a week for 13 weeks, with one realistic case, a linked BABOK® knowledge graph, and an AI instructor.


                  
                  What's inside 
                  
                


The course: 75 lessons in 9 modules. Each one follows teach → apply → exam drill → wrap-up.
The knowledge graph: 228 linked notes covering 6 knowledge areas, 30 tasks, their inputs and outputs, 50 techniques, competencies and perspectives, plus an exam lens.
The GreenBasket scenario: you are the Senior BA on a grocery chain’s Click & Collect initiative, from the messy kickoff to pilot evaluation.
The 13-week roadmap: phases, milestones, and the weekly rhythm.



How to use it

Business Analysis Core Concept Model (BACCM)


                  
                  Six equal concepts 
                  
                

Each core concept is defined by the other five and none is more important than another. If any one changes, re-evaluate the others and their relationship to value. (BABOK 2.1, p.12)

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.title: Change
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.content:
Change


                  
                  Definition (in our words; see BABOK 2.1) 
                  
                

A transformation made in response to a need.


Changes are deliberate and controlled through business analysis, aiming to improve how the enterprise performs.
Ask: What kind of change are we making?
Part of BACCM · related: Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.title: Context
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.content:
Context


                  
                  Definition (in our words; see BABOK 2.1) 
                  
                

The surrounding circumstances that shape the change, are shaped by it, and help explain it.


Everything relevant to the change within the environment: attitudes, culture, competitors, governments, infrastructure, processes, technology, weather…
Ask: What surrounds the change and the solution?
Part of BACCM · related: Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.title: Need
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.content:
Need


                  
                  Definition (in our words; see BABOK 2.1) 
                  
                

A problem to solve or an opportunity to pursue.


A need can trigger change by prompting stakeholders to act. A change can also create new needs when it raises or lowers the value of existing solutions.
Ask: Which problem or opportunity are we addressing?
Part of BACCM · related: Change, Solution, Stakeholder, Value, Context

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.title: Solution
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.content:
Solution


                  
                  Definition (in our words; see BABOK 2.1) 
                  
                

A particular way of meeting one or more needs within a context.


A solution meets a need by solving a problem or letting stakeholders exploit an opportunity.
Ask: What are we building or changing to meet the need?
Part of BACCM · related: Change, Need, Stakeholder, Value, Context

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.title: Stakeholder
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.content:
Stakeholder


                  
                  Definition (in our words; see BABOK 2.1) 
                  
                

Anyone (individual or group) connected to the change, the need or the solution.


Usually described by their interest in, impact from, and influence over the change. See the 11 generic Stakeholder Roles.
Ask: Who is involved or affected?
Part of BACCM · related: Change, Need, Solution, Value, Context

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.title: Value
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Core-Conc.content:
Value


                  
                  Definition (in our words; see BABOK 2.1) 
                  
                

How much something is worth, or how important or useful it is, to a stakeholder in a given context.


Can be tangible (directly measurable, often monetary) or intangible (measured indirectly, e.g. reputation, morale); potential or realized; absolute or relative. Losses, risks and costs are negative value.
Ask: What does each stakeholder regard as valuable?
Part of BACCM · related: Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Context

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Key-Terms.title: Key Terms
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Key-Terms.content:
Key Terms (BABOK 2.2)
Business Analysis
The practice of making change happen in an enterprise by clarifying needs and proposing solutions that create value for stakeholders.
Business Analysis Information
Any information, at any level of detail, that business analysis uses or produces, such as elicitation results, requirements, designs, solution options, solution scope and change strategy.
Design
A usable representation of a solution. It shows how value could be realized if the solution were built.
Enterprise
One or more organizations, together with the solutions they use, pursuing shared goals. Its boundary is drawn around the change, not around a legal entity.
Organization
An autonomous group under a single management that works towards common goals on an ongoing basis, unlike a temporary project team.
Plan
A proposal for achieving something: events, dependencies, sequence, schedule, results, resources and people.
Requirement
A usable representation of a need. It focuses on the kind of value that fulfilling it could bring.
Risk
How uncertainty affects the value of a change, a solution or the enterprise. It can be reduced, removed, avoided, shared, accepted, or (for opportunities) increased.


                  
                  Exam lens 
                  
                

Requirement ↔ need, design ↔ solution. BABOK widened “requirements” to “business analysis information” so that every input/output is covered by the tasks.


Related: Requirements and Designs · Requirements Classification Schema · BACCM

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Requireme.title: Requirements Classification Schema
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Requireme.content:
Requirements Classification Schema (BABOK 2.3)
graph TD
  BR[Business Requirements<br/>WHY: goals, objectives, outcomes] --> SR[Stakeholder Requirements<br/>needs of stakeholders]
  SR --> SolR[Solution Requirements<br/>capabilities & qualities]
  SolR --> FR[Functional]
  SolR --> NFR[Non-functional / quality of service]
  TR[Transition Requirements<br/>temporary: data conversion, training, continuity]
  SolR -.-> TR




































TypeWhat it describesExampleBusinessGoals, objectives and outcomes — why the change was initiated (enterprise, business area, or initiative level).Increase online sales by 15% in 12 months.StakeholderNeeds of stakeholders that must be met to achieve business requirements; bridge between business and solution requirements.Store managers need a daily view of stock levels.Solution – functionalCapabilities: the behaviour and information the solution manages.The system shall send an order confirmation email.Solution – non-functionalConditions under which the solution must remain effective, or qualities it must have.Pages load in under 2 seconds for 95% of requests.TransitionCapabilities/conditions needed only to move from current to future state; temporary.Migrate 5 years of order history; train 200 staff.


                  
                  Exam lens 
                  
                

Transition requirements are the only temporary type. Business requirements originate in Analyze Current State as Business Requirements. NFRs are analysed with Non-Functional Requirements Analysis.


Study guides: Lessing pp.59–62 · Jonasson ch.8 (RADD) pp.169–172

knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Requireme.title: Requirements and Designs
knowledge-graph/01-Foundations/Requireme.content:
Requirements and Designs (BABOK 2.5)

Requirements focus on the need; designs focus on the solution.
Both are elicited, modelled and analyzed with the same techniques. Requirements lead to designs, and designs often surface further requirements. The cycle repeats until the need is met.
Tasks like Trace Requirements or Specify and Model Requirements refer to requirements, but include designs.
The BA keeps asking “why?” to turn a stakeholder’s stated solution into the underlying need.

knowledge-graph/02-Knowledge-Areas/Busin.content:
Business Analysis Planning and Monitoring (BAPM)


                  
                  Exam weight: 14% of CBAP questions (≈17 of 120)
                  
                

Plan HOW business analysis will be done: approach, stakeholders, governance, information management, and continuous improvement of BA work itself.


Tasks



































TaskPurposeOutputs3.1 Plan Business Analysis ApproachDecide how business analysis will be carried out on this initiative: the overall method, its formality, the activities, their timing, and how the approach gets agreed.Business Analysis Approach3.2 Plan Stakeholder EngagementWork out who the stakeholders are, what they are like, and how the BA will work and communicate with each of them.Stakeholder Engagement Approach3.3 Plan Business Analysis GovernanceSet the rules for decisions about requirements and designs: who decides, how changes are controlled, how priorities are set, and how approvals happen.Governance Approach3.4 Plan Business Analysis Information ManagementDecide how business analysis information will be organized, detailed, traced, reused, stored and described with attributes.Information Management Approach3.5 Identify Business Analysis Performance ImprovementsEvaluate how well the business analysis work itself is going, and put improvements in place.Business Analysis Performance Assessment

                  Exam lens 
                  
                


Its outputs are mostly approaches that act as guidelines for nearly every other task — know the five outputs by heart.
Only KA whose inputs include something “external” at the start: Needs and Performance Objectives (external).
Questions often ask “what should the BA do FIRST” — planning/tailoring the approach usually precedes elicitation.
Predictive vs adaptive trade-offs (formality, timing, level of detail) are heavily tested.

Requirements Life Cycle Management (RLCM)


                  
                  Exam weight: 15% of CBAP questions (≈18 of 120)
                  
                

Manage and maintain requirements and designs from inception to retirement: trace, maintain, prioritize, assess changes, approve.


Tasks



































TaskPurposeOutputs5.1 Trace RequirementsLink requirements and designs across levels so that alignment, coverage and the impact of changes are visible.Requirements (traced), Designs (traced)5.2 Maintain RequirementsKeep requirements correct, consistent and well-attributed over their whole life, and make them reusable.Requirements (maintained), Designs (maintained)5.3 Prioritize RequirementsRank requirements and designs by relative importance, with stakeholders, and keep doing so as things change.Requirements (prioritized), Designs (prioritized)5.4 Assess Requirements ChangesWork out what a proposed change to requirements or designs would mean (benefit, cost, impact, schedule, urgency) and resolve it through governance.Requirements Change Assessment, Designs Change Assessment5.5 Approve RequirementsReach agreement and approval on requirements and designs so that work can continue.Requirements (approved), Designs (approved)

Solution Evaluation (SE)


                  
                  Exam weight: 14% of CBAP questions (≈17 of 120)
                  
                

Assess the performance and value of a solution in use (or being built) and recommend actions to increase value.


Tasks

knowledge-graph/08-Exam-Lens/Commonly-Co.title: Commonly Confused Concepts
knowledge-graph/08-Exam-Lens/Commonly-Co.content:
Commonly Confused Concepts
Pairs that exam distractors exploit.
Verify Requirements vs Validate Requirements
Verify = quality of the requirement itself (well-formed, testable, unambiguous) — “built right”. Validate = requirement aligns with business need and delivers value — “right thing”.
Confirm Elicitation Results vs Verify Requirements
Confirm checks the BA understood stakeholders correctly (4.3). Verify checks requirement quality (7.2).
Solution Limitation vs Enterprise Limitation
Solution limitation = inside the solution (8.3). Enterprise limitation = culture, structure, operations outside the solution (8.4).
Business Requirements vs Business Objectives
Business requirements (6.1) state the need/why. Business objectives (6.2) are SMART, measurable targets for the future state.
Change Strategy vs Solution Scope
Both are outputs of 6.4. Change strategy = HOW the enterprise transitions; solution scope = WHAT the solution includes.
Potential Value vs Solution Recommendation
Potential value (6.2) = value expected from the future state. Solution recommendation (7.6) = the option chosen as most valuable.
Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria vs Metrics and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
Criteria assess or accept a solution at a point in time; KPIs measure ongoing performance against goals.
Business Analysis Performance Assessment vs Solution Performance Analysis
The first measures the BA work (3.5); the second measures the solution (8.2).
Stakeholder Engagement Approach vs Stakeholder Engagement
Approach = the plan (3.2). Stakeholder Engagement = the outcome of ongoing collaboration (4.5).
Data Flow Diagrams vs Process Modelling
DFD shows how DATA moves and is transformed (no sequence/decisions). Process models show sequence of activities and decisions.
Business Rules Analysis vs Decision Modelling
Rules analysis captures individual rules (definitional vs behavioural). Decision modelling shows how rules combine into a repeatable decision.
Focus Groups vs Workshops
Focus groups gather opinions/attitudes (qualitative, not decisions). Workshops produce decisions/agreement on a defined outcome.
Concept Modelling vs Data Modelling
Concept model = business vocabulary, independent of implementation. Data model = entities, attributes, relationships toward design.
Glossary vs Data Dictionary
Glossary defines business terms. Data dictionary defines data elements (type, values, composition).

Exam-day heuristics

Read the LAST sentence of a case question first — it tells you what is asked (task, technique, output, next step).
Pick the “most BABOK” answer: the one that follows the task’s purpose and uses its inputs/outputs, even if another answer works in real life.
State labels on outputs are clues: unconfirmed → confirmed; specified & modelled → verified → validated/prioritized → approved.
When stuck between two plausible answers, prefer the one that involves stakeholders / collaboration and addresses value.
Know which task PRODUCES each output and which tasks CONSUME it — it answers “what comes next” questions.
