scenario/case-files/01-sponsor-kickoff-e.title: 01-sponsor-kickoff-email
scenario/case-files/01-sponsor-kickoff-e.content:
From: Elena Marsh (COO)
To: Grace Nwosu; Tom Okafor; [you]
Cc: David Chen; Marcus Lee; Helen Kowalski
Subject: Click & Collect – let’s get it right this time
Team,
Welcome aboard to our new Senior BA. You’re joining at exactly the right moment.
The board was clear last week: we are losing customers to FreshWay and QuickCart because they let people order online and pick up in store (FreshWay also delivers). We have lost about 4 share points in two years and our loyalty members are shopping less often: visit frequency is down 11% year-on-year.
I want customers to be able to order on our app or website and collect at their local store within 2 hours. I want it live in at least 6 stores within 6 months and chain-wide within 12. Online should be 5% of sales within 2 years of full launch.
Some things I already know we need:

A slick app, better than FreshWay’s.
Real-time stock, so customers never order something we don’t have.
Loyalty points on online orders.
Parking bays with signage at each store.
Pickers must never have to walk more than one lap of the store per order.
Probably ShelfWise. Their demo was impressive and they say 10 weeks to launch.

I know Harvest left scars. Marcus, I need your stores on board from day one this time. David, the $3.2M is approved but I expect a proper business case before we sign any vendor.
Can the BA team come back to me in two weeks with how you’re going to approach this? No 80-page documents please.
Elena

P.S. Lily’s team is already asking about recipes and personalized offers in the app. Park that for now unless it’s cheap.

scenario/case-files/02-harvest-postmorte.title: 02-harvest-postmortem
scenario/case-files/02-harvest-postmorte.content:
Project Harvest: Post-Mortem (DRAFT, never formally approved)
Author: former PMO analyst · March 2025 · Status: “draft v3 – do not circulate”
Summary
Harvest aimed to launch online ordering with home delivery and in-store pickup in 10 stores. After 14 months and $1.8M, the project was cancelled 3 weeks before the pilot go-live.
Timeline

Jan 2024: Kick-off. The vendor (CodeHarbor) was selected by the CIO at the time, based on a demo.
Feb–Apr 2024: Requirements. A 212-page specification was written by the vendor’s analysts in 6 weeks. HQ workshops only; no store staff invited (“to avoid disrupting operations”).
May–Nov 2024: Build. 63 change requests were raised, and 41 of them came from stakeholders who saw the product for the first time in UAT.
Dec 2024: Trial picks in 2 stores. Average pick time was 38 minutes per 30-item order (target 15). Out-of-stock at pick was 19%.
Feb 2025: Cancelled by the new COO (Elena Marsh).

What went wrong (as recorded)

Requirements were “signed off” by the sponsor’s delegate without the stores reviewing them. No one owned approvals.
The spec mixed business needs with screen designs. Nobody could tell why a feature existed.
Stock data from StockPoint was assumed to be accurate. It wasn’t (about 82%).
Store managers were “informed” by email one week before the trial.
Delivery added cost and complexity (vans, drivers, insurance) for low demand in suburban areas.
There was no change control process. Changes were agreed in corridors.
There were no success measures defined, so no one could say whether the trial was working.
Union consultation was not started. HR learned about the new “picker” role from a store manager.

What went right

The customer-facing web prototype tested well with 20 loyalty members (NPS +41).
The integration adapter for TillMaster worked and could be reused.
Kim Tran (Riverton Central) wrote an excellent list of picking problems. It was never acted on. (Attached below.)

Attachment: Picker issues list (Kim Tran, Dec 2024)

Items not on the shelf the system says they’re on. Aisle locations are out of date after resets.
No guidance on substitutions, so every picker decides differently.
The handheld battery lasts about 2 hours.
Chilled items picked first were warm by the end.
Picking during the Saturday rush means fighting customers for trolleys.
Nobody told us whether picking counts in our productivity targets.

Open actions (never closed)

Decide the delivery vs pickup strategy
Fix inventory accuracy
Define an owner for product master data

scenario/case-files/03-store-ops-process.title: 03-store-ops-process-notes
scenario/case-files/03-store-ops-process.content:
Store Operations: How a Customer “Phone Order” Works Today
Source: Store Operations manual, section 7.4 (last updated 2019), plus handwritten margin notes from Riverton Central

Several stores informally accept phone orders from elderly customers and local businesses (≈ 40–80 orders/week chain-wide). There is no system support.

Official process (manual 7.4)

The customer calls the store’s customer service desk.
The desk associate writes the order on form SO-12 (paper, in triplicate).
The order is placed in the “orders tray” and picked by the next available associate before 5 pm.
Chilled and frozen items are picked last and stored in the back-room cooler.
The customer arrives, and the desk associate retrieves the order and rings it through the POS at the desk till.
Payment is taken at pickup (card or cash).
The white copy of SO-12 is filed for 30 days.

Margin notes (Rosa Delgado)

“Step 3 never happens before 5. Usually the night shift picks it.”
“We ring it up on the main tills, not the desk till. The desk till is broken half the time.”
“Substitutions: we call the customer if we can. Mrs. Olsen says ‘use your judgement’.”
“Frozen goes straight to the ice-cream freezer at the front. The back cooler is full of flowers on Fridays.”
“No alcohol on phone orders. Head office rule, but nobody wrote it down.”

scenario/case-files/04-customer-feedback.title: 04-customer-feedback-q2
scenario/case-files/04-customer-feedback.content:
Customer Feedback: Q2 extract (app store reviews, contact centre, loyalty survey verbatims)

“Love the store, hate that I can’t order ahead. Switched my big weekly shop to QuickCart.” (Loyalty survey, member 7 yrs)
“Your app only shows points. Why can’t I build a list and just collect it?” (App review, 2★)
“FreshWay substituted my oat milk with regular milk. Never again. If you do online, ASK me first.” (Survey)
“I don’t do apps. Can I phone my order in like I used to at the Maple St store?” (Contact centre)
“Pickup should be fast. If I have to wait more than 5 minutes in the car park, what’s the point?” (Survey)
“Would pay a small fee for a 1-hour slot.” (Survey, 23 similar mentions)
“Please show allergens online. My son has a nut allergy.” (Survey, 14 similar mentions)

IT Landscape: Systems Relevant to Click & Collect (Anil Kapoor, Enterprise Architecture)
[TillMaster POS v9] --real-time--> [Basket Rewards (loyalty, cloud)]
        |                                   |

[Product master data: Category team spreadsheets]
[Brochure website (CMS)]      [Payment gateway: PayRail (card-present only today)]
[Workforce scheduling: RosterPro]   [Handhelds: 2016 models, ~40% failing]

Key facts

StockPoint has no API. The only way out is a nightly flat-file export. The vendor offers a paid “Connect” API module ($180k and 5 months).
Inventory accuracy is 82% on average: 91% in dry grocery, 74% in fresh/chilled.
Aisle location data exists for 60% of SKUs and goes stale after planogram resets (every 6–8 weeks).
TillMaster can accept “pre-paid order” transactions with a firmware upgrade (v9.4). The Harvest adapter is reusable.
PayRail supports online card-not-present payments, but it puts the web channel in PCI-DSS scope unless a hosted payment page is used.
Basket Rewards has an API for earning and burning points. Digital coupons are not exposed through the API.
Handhelds: a replacement is budgeted for next fiscal year only.
Security: all new SaaS must pass a vendor security assessment (6–8 weeks).

Anil’s warning
“Whatever we choose, real-time stock is a myth with StockPoint. Near-real-time at best, and only if we fix the data first.”

scenario/case-files/08-compliance-memo.title: 08-compliance-memo
scenario/case-files/08-compliance-memo.content:
MEMO: Compliance considerations for Click & Collect
From: Janet Brooks, Chief Compliance & Privacy Officer

Privacy. Online accounts will collect personal data (name, phone, email, order history). This needs a privacy notice, explicit consent for marketing, and data retention of no more than 24 months for order history unless the customer opts in. Personalized offers based on purchase history require opt-in consent.
Payments. Card data must never touch GreenBasket servers. Use a hosted payment page or tokenization to keep PCI-DSS scope minimal.
Food safety (state regulations). Chilled items must be held at 5°C or below and frozen at −18°C or below from pick to handover. Temperature must be logged at least every 4 hours, and logs kept for 12 months. Hot food is out of scope.
Alcohol. 29 stores sell alcohol. Age must be verified with photo ID at handover by a staff member aged 18 or over, and refusal must be logged. In State C, alcohol cannot be handed over between 11 pm and 7 am. The customer’s ID cannot be stored.
Accessibility. Digital channels must meet WCAG 2.1 AA (corporate policy since 2023).
Union agreement (with HR). New or changed duties for store staff need 45 days’ consultation in States A and B.

“I don’t need to be in every meeting, but I need to see anything touching these six areas before approval.”

Interview Transcript: Rosa Delgado, Store Manager, Riverton Central
Conducted by: previous BA contractor (Harvest), Nov 2024. Unreviewed.
Q: How do phone orders work today?
Rosa: The desk takes them on the SO-12 form, someone picks them in the afternoon, the chilled goes in the back cooler, and the customer pays at the desk till when they come in.
Q: How long does picking take?
Rosa: About 15 minutes for a normal order.
Q: What would make online pickup work?
Rosa: A dedicated picker in the morning. Not at the Saturday peak, that’s chaos. And a staging area. The back cooler is too small.
Q: Stock accuracy?
Rosa: Mostly fine. Dry goods are good. Fresh is a guess.
Q: Alcohol?
Rosa: People would love it. We’d need someone over 18 at the pickup desk. Most of the evening staff are students, some are 17.
Q: Anything else?
Rosa: Don’t let head office design this alone again. Talk to Kim. Kim knows.

Contractor’s summary: “Store confirms current process is per manual 7.4. Pick time ~15 min. Stock accuracy acceptable. Alcohol feasible.”

Observations

Two stores (Riverton Central, Oakfield) hit nearly every target. Two (Bayview, Hillcrest) are well below.
Most accuracy errors are items shown as “in stock” that were not on the shelf. The 15-minute stock sync works, but StockPoint itself is wrong for fresh items.

scenario/company-context/COMPANY.content:
GreenBasket Markets: Company Profile









































FactValueFounded1987, family-owned until 2015; now majority-owned by a private equity fundStores42 (31 full-size, 11 “GreenBasket Express” convenience) in 3 statesAnnual revenue$1.1BEmployees~6,800 (about 85% in stores); store staff are represented by a union in 2 of the 3 statesLoyalty program”Basket Rewards”, 410,000 active members, points-based, app plus cardMarket share (home region)18.2% in 2023 → 14.1% nowOnline sales0%. The two largest competitors report 9–12% of sales online.Strategic goal (board)“Protect and grow our customer base by making GreenBasket the most convenient neighbourhood grocer”
How the business runs today

Store operations are decentralized. Store managers have a lot of autonomy over layout, staffing and local promotions.
Inventory is tracked in StockPoint, an on-premise inventory system from 2011. It is updated by nightly batch from the POS. Cycle counts are done monthly. Measured inventory record accuracy is 82% (industry leaders are above 95%).
POS is TillMaster v9, with a real-time transaction feed only to the loyalty system.
Product master data (names, images, sizes, allergens) is kept in spreadsheets by the Category team. About 30% of SKUs have no image. Allergen data is incomplete.
E-commerce: the website is a brochure site with store locator and weekly flyers. The Basket Rewards app shows points and digital coupons only.
Fresh & cold chain: food safety regulation requires chilled items to stay at 5°C or below and frozen items at −18°C or below, with temperature logs.
Alcohol is sold in 29 stores. It needs age verification at handover, and state rules differ.
Payments: card processing through a PCI-DSS compliant provider. Online card payment has never been done.

scenario/company-context/SCENARIO.title: SCENARIO
scenario/company-context/SCENARIO.content:
The Scenario: GreenBasket “Click & Collect”
Your role
You have just joined GreenBasket Markets as a Senior Business Analyst. You report to the Director of the Transformation Office and have been assigned to the company’s most visible initiative of the year.
The situation
GreenBasket is a regional grocery chain with 42 stores. In two years it has lost about 4 points of market share to competitors that offer online ordering with store pickup or delivery. GreenBasket offers neither.
The board wants a “Click & Collect” capability: customers order online and pick up at a store. The COO is sponsoring it, and the board has given the executive team 12 months to show results.
There is history. A previous attempt, Project Harvest (2024), spent $1.8M and was cancelled before launch. People are wary, stores are sceptical, and the files it left behind are a mess.
The arc (it follows your 13-week study plan)









































Study phaseWhat happens at GreenBasketFoundations (wk 1–2)You read the inherited files and learn who’s who.BA Planning & Monitoring (wk 3)You plan how business analysis will work on this initiative.Elicitation & Collaboration (wk 4)You interview, observe, and run workshops with stores, IT and customers.Requirements Life Cycle Mgmt (wk 5)You trace, prioritize, handle a disruptive change request, and get approvals.Strategy Analysis (wk 6)You define current state, future state, risks, and the change strategy (business case).RADD (wk 7–8)You model, verify, validate and architect requirements, then recommend a vendor option.Solution Evaluation (wk 9)A 6-store pilot has run. You measure it, find the limitations, and recommend actions.Consolidation & exam (wk 10–13)You review everything as an examiner would.
Where things live

scenario/company-context/stakeholders/ST.title: STAKEHOLDERS
scenario/company-context/stakeholders/ST.content:
Stakeholder Profiles
Use these profiles when you role-play elicitation and when you analyze stakeholders. The BABOK role is given in brackets. The lessons ask you to confirm or challenge it.

Elena Marsh, COO [Sponsor]

Launched the initiative and controls the budget ($3.2M approved, with a contingency request pending) and the scope.
Wants: a visible result within 12 months, and no repeat of Harvest.
Style: decisive, impatient with detail, wants one-page summaries and clear options.
Attitude: champion. High power, high interest.
Hidden concern: her credibility with the board is tied to this.

David Chen, CFO [Sponsor-adjacent / decision maker on investment]

Approves any spending above $500k and any change to the business case.
Wants: payback within 3 years and a clear NPV.
Attitude: sceptical after Harvest. High power, medium interest.

Marcus Lee, Head of Store Operations [Domain SME, key influencer]

Runs 42 stores and has 22 years with GreenBasket.
Wants: no extra burden on store staff, and protection of store P&L.
Attitude: resistant. Harvest ignored his teams and he “told them it would fail”. High power, high interest. Can block adoption.
Communication: prefers face-to-face and distrusts slide decks.

Rosa Delgado, Store Manager, Riverton Central [Domain SME / End user representative]

Best-run store in the chain and a likely pilot store. Knows every workaround.
Wants: a process that works during the Saturday peak, and enough staff.
Attitude: curious but cautious. Medium power, high interest. Informal influencer among store managers.

Kim Tran, Store Associate / picker, Riverton Central [End user]

4 years’ experience; did the Harvest trial picks in 2024.
Knows: why picking was slow (items not where the system said, no substitutions guidance, handheld scanners dying).
Attitude: open, and will speak honestly if it feels safe. Low power, high interest.

Anil Kapoor, Enterprise Architect [Implementation SME]

Knows StockPoint, TillMaster and every integration pain.
Wants: a clean integration architecture and no custom spaghetti.
Attitude: supportive but warns about inventory data quality. Medium power.

Helen Kowalski, CIO [Implementation SME / approver for technology decisions]

Must approve the solution architecture and vendor selection. Worries about cybersecurity and PCI scope.

Janet Brooks, Chief Compliance & Privacy Officer [Regulator (internal)]

Enforces privacy law, PCI-DSS, food-safety cold chain rules and alcohol sale rules.
Attitude: neutral and precise. Can stop a launch. High power, low-to-medium interest until something touches her domains.

External regulators [Regulator]

State food safety agency (cold chain, temperature logging), state liquor authorities (age verification), and the payment card industry (PCI-DSS via the acquirer).

Tom Okafor, Project Manager [Project Manager]

Owns schedule, budget and resources. Wants a stable scope early and fears scope creep.

Priyanka Rao, QA Lead [Tester]

Wants testable requirements with acceptance criteria. Reviews requirements for quality.

Dev Patel, IT Service Desk Manager [Operational Support]

Will support the solution after go-live. Wants runbooks, monitoring, and store-friendly error messages.

Lily Park, Head of Digital Marketing [Domain SME]

Wants flashy features: recipes, personalized offers, a same-day delivery “later”. High interest, medium power. Adds scope.

Ben Adeyemi, Category Management Lead [Domain SME]

Owns product master data (images, allergens, sizes). Under-resourced.

Owen Fitzgerald, Supply Chain Director [Domain SME]

Owns replenishment and distribution centres. Cares about inventory accuracy and cold chain.

Nadia Kowal, HR Director [Domain SME]

Handles union relations. Any change to store roles or duties needs a union consultation in 2 states (45-day notice).

Customers [Customer]

Persona “Busy Parent Sam”: two kids, orders weekly, values reliability over price, hates substitutions without asking.
Persona “Retired Margaret”: loyal in-store shopper, wary of apps, wants phone support.
Persona “Young Professional Jay”: compares competitors, expects real-time availability and a pickup slot within 2 hours.

Vendors [Supplier]

ShelfWise: SaaS click-and-collect platform, fast to deploy, subscription pricing, limited customization.
CodeHarbor: custom development agency (the same agency that built Harvest).
OmniGrocer Suite: hybrid packaged platform with configurable modules and an integration layer.
